beauty.question: What is beauty? Is it in things themselves, or in the eye of the beholder? And what is art for?

stops.text: In the Symposium, Socrates describes a ladder of beauty: from one beautiful body, to all beautiful bodies, to beautiful souls, laws and knowledge, and finally to beauty itself, eternal and pure. For Plato, beauty draws the soul upward toward the truth.

Plotinus asks why things are beautiful. Not just because of symmetry, he says, since a single color or a simple sound can be beautiful too. Beauty is a form shining through matter, and the soul loves it because it recognizes its own home.

As Dante rises through Heaven, Beatrice grows more beautiful with each sphere, and the light grows brighter. Beauty becomes a sign of God's glory. At the end, Dante's words fail before the beauty he sees.

quote.text: His glory, by whose might all things are mov'd, Pierces the universe, and in one part Sheds more resplendence, elsewhere less. ...
quote.author: Dante
quote.ed: The Vision, London

stops.text: Shakespeare's sonnets praise a friend's beauty and worry that time will destroy it. Their answer is that the poem will keep that beauty alive as long as people read. Beauty fades, but art can preserve it.

quote.text: Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.ed: Shake-speares Sonnets, London

stops.text: Kepler finds beauty in mathematics and in the heavens. He compares the planets' speeds to musical intervals and imagines a harmony of the spheres. For him, the beauty of the cosmos showed the mind of its maker.

Kant says that when we call something beautiful, we mean more than 'I like it': we expect others to agree, though we can't prove it by rules. Beauty pleases freely, without serving any use. He also describes the sublime, the awe we feel before vast mountains or storms.

quote.text: The beautiful is that which pleases universally, without a concept.
quote.author: Immanuel Kant
quote.ed: Kant's Critique of Judgement, 2nd edition, revised, Macmillan, London

stops.text: Dr. Astrov plants forests and worries about their destruction. He says forests teach people about beauty and lift their minds. Chekhov lets beauty in nature stand against the dullness of the characters' lives.

quote.text: He says that forests are the ornaments of the earth, that they teach mankind to understand beauty and attune his mind to lofty sentiments.
quote.author: Chekhov
quote.ed: Plays by Anton Tchekoff (Charles Scribner's Sons, New York)

stops.text: Huizinga describes the late Middle Ages through its colors, ceremonies, art and sounds. He shows how beauty filled everyday life, from painted books to the ringing of church bells. Art, for him, is a key to understanding a whole age.

quote.text: One sound rose ceaselessly above the noises of busy life and lifted all things unto a sphere of order and serenity: the sound of bells.
quote.author: Johan Huizinga
quote.work: The Waning of the Middle Ages, Chapter I
quote.ed: Edward Arnold, London

stops.text: The mathematician G. H. Hardy argues that beauty is the first test of good mathematics. A beautiful proof is surprising, simple and inevitable. He compares the mathematician to a painter or a poet, a maker of patterns.

young: What do you think is beautiful? A sunset, a flower, a song, a kind face? Beauty is something that makes us stop and say 'wow.'

People have argued for ages whether beauty is in the thing itself or in the eye of the person looking. Kant noticed that when we say something is beautiful, we hope others will see it too. Share something you think is beautiful with someone today.
talk: What is the most beautiful thing you have ever seen?
Is beauty in the thing or in the eye of the beholder?
Can math be beautiful? Can a good deed be beautiful?
Why do people make art?
Shakespeare said poems keep beauty alive. How else do we keep beautiful things?

cause.question: Why do things happen? Do events have causes and purposes, or does chance play a part?

stops.text: The Hippocratic doctors look for natural causes of disease: winds, water, seasons, diet. They reject explanations by the anger of gods. Finding the cause, they believed, is the first step toward a cure.

quote.text: Men regard its nature and cause as divine from ignorance and wonder, because it is not at all like to other diseases.
quote.author: Hippocrates (Hippocratic Corpus)
quote.ed: Sydenham Society, London

stops.text: Aristotle names four kinds of cause: what a thing is made of, its form, what started it, and what it is for. A statue's bronze, its shape, its sculptor and its purpose all help explain it. He thought nature too acts for ends, as an acorn grows toward an oak.

quote.text: Again (4) in the sense of end or 'that for the sake of which' a thing is done, e.g. health is the cause of walking about.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.tr: R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye
quote.ed: Oxford, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Lucretius explains everything by atoms moving and colliding, with no purposes and no gods steering. To leave room for free will, he says atoms sometimes swerve slightly, by chance. Nature, for him, is cause and chance, not plan.

Aquinas argues that a chain of causes can't go back forever without a first cause, and that things in nature act for ends as if directed. He calls the first cause and director God. He also holds that God works through natural causes, which science can study.

quote.text: Therefore some intelligent being exists by whom all natural things are directed to their end; and this being we call God.
quote.author: Thomas Aquinas
quote.work: Summa Theologica, First Part, Question 2, Article 3 (the fifth way)
quote.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province
quote.ed: Second and Revised Edition

stops.text: Spinoza holds that everything follows necessarily from the nature of God, or Nature, as a theorem follows from geometry. There is no chance and no purpose in the usual sense. Understanding the causes of things, he thinks, brings peace.

Hume asks what we really see when one billiard ball strikes another. We see one motion followed by another, but never the power that links them. Our idea of cause, he argues, comes from habit after seeing the same thing happen again and again.

quote.text: May not the first ball return in a straight line, or leap off from the second in any line or direction?
quote.author: David Hume
quote.ed: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, reprinted from the edition of 1777, Open Court, Chicago

stops.text: Voltaire mocks Dr. Pangloss, who insists that everything happens for the best, no matter how terrible. Pangloss finds a purpose for everything, even noses made to hold spectacles. Voltaire's target was a kind of easy optimism about causes and purposes.

quote.text: Observe, that the nose has been formed to bear spectacles—thus we have spectacles."
quote.author: Voltaire
quote.ed: Candide, The Modern Library, Boni and Liveright, New York

stops.text: Tolstoy asks what caused Napoleon's invasion of Russia. Not Napoleon alone, he answers, but millions of causes in millions of people. Historians who name one cause are, in his view, fooling themselves.

Heisenberg explains that in quantum physics, single events like an atom's decay can be predicted only as probabilities. Chance seems built into nature at the smallest scale. Physicists still debate what that means.

young: A cause is what makes something happen. If you drop a glass, the glass breaks. The drop is the cause; the broken glass is the effect.
Aristotle asked four 'why' questions about a thing: What is it made of? What shape is it? Who or what made it? What is it for? Try them on your toothbrush!
talk: Ask Aristotle's four questions about a chair. What are the answers?
Is anything really an accident, or does everything have a cause?
Hume says we never see the cause itself, only one thing after another. Is he right?
Pangloss thought everything happens for the best. What did Voltaire think of that?
What caused something good that happened to you this week?

character.question: Where does good character come from? Can goodness be taught, or is it built by practice, or is it a gift?

stances.label: Virtue as a kind of knowledge
Virtue built by practice and habit
Goodness as a gift of God's grace
Habit and grace together

character.stance_note: Uncolored stops take up character in other ways.

stops.text: Meno asks Socrates whether virtue can be taught. Socrates leans toward the view that virtue is a kind of wisdom, since no one does wrong knowing it is bad for them. But he also notices that good fathers often fail to teach their sons, and the dialogue ends with the puzzle still open, suggesting that good people may have their goodness as a gift of the gods.

quote.text: Can you tell me, Socrates, whether virtue is acquired by teaching or by practice; or if neither by teaching nor by practice, then whether it comes to man by nature, or in what other way?
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Aristotle answers that character virtues come from practice. We become brave by doing brave things, the way a builder learns by building. Each virtue is a settled habit of choosing the middle path between too much and too little, guided by practical wisdom.

quote.text: And so by doing just acts we become just, and by doing acts of temperance and courage we become temperate and courageous.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: Kegan Paul

stops.text: Plutarch writes lives, not histories, so that readers can see character up close: in small sayings and choices as well as in battles. He believes that seeing a good action told well makes us want to do likewise. His paired lives of Greeks and Romans are meant as mirrors for the reader.

quote.text: But virtue, by the bare statement of its actions, can so affect men’s minds as to create at once both admiration of the things done and desire to imitate the doers of them.
quote.author: Plutarch
quote.tr: John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough
quote.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 12, P. F. Collier & Son

stops.text: Augustine tells how he knew what was good for years and still could not make himself do it. His will was divided against itself. He came to believe that only God's grace could heal the will, and that a person cannot become good by effort alone.

Aquinas joins Aristotle and Augustine. The moral virtues, such as courage and self-control, can be gained by practice, as Aristotle taught. But faith, hope and charity, which direct a person to God, are in his view given by God, and charity is the form that gives all the other virtues their full worth.

quote.text: It is therefore evident that hope is a virtue, since it causes a human act to be good and to attain its due rule.
quote.author: Thomas Aquinas
quote.work: Summa Theologica, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 17, Article 1
quote.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province
quote.ed: Second and Revised Edition

stops.text: Machiavelli uses the word virtù for a ruler's boldness, skill and readiness to act, which is not the same as moral goodness. He advises that a prince who wants to keep power must learn to be able not to be good when needed. Readers have argued for centuries over whether he was describing politics as it is or recommending it.

Kant says the one thing good without any qualification is a good will. Talents, courage and even happiness can be used badly. What gives an act its moral worth, in his view, is that it is done because it is right, not because it is pleasant or useful.

quote.text: Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good without qualification, except a Good Will.
quote.author: Immanuel Kant
quote.ed: Kant's Critique of Practical Reason and Other Works on the Theory of Ethics, 4th edition, Longmans, Green, London

stops.text: Jane Austen's Emma is clever and kind but sure of her own judgment, and she meddles in her friends' lives. Her character grows through mistakes and through a friend willing to tell her the truth. Austen shows virtue being learned in ordinary life, in visits, conversations and apologies.

quote.text: Knightley, in fact, was one of the few people who could see faults in Emma Woodhouse, and the only one who ever told her of them ...
quote.author: Austen
quote.ed: John Murray, London (first edition)

stops.text: William James brings Aristotle's point into the age of science. Habits, he explains, are paths worn into the nervous system by repetition. So we should make good actions automatic early, start new habits strongly, and never allow an exception until the habit is firm.

quote.text: The great thing, then, in all education, is to make our nervous system our ally instead of our enemy.
quote.author: William James
quote.work: The Principles of Psychology, Chapter IV (Habit)
quote.ed: Henry Holt and Company, New York

young: Character is the kind of person you are when you choose what to do. Are you kind? Do you tell the truth? Do you keep trying when something is hard?

Aristotle says you get good character the way you get good at piano or soccer: by practicing. Every time you share, or tell the truth when it is hard, it gets a little easier next time. Some writers add that we also need help from others, and many believe we need help from God.
talk: Can you learn to be kind the way you learn to read? What would the lessons be?
Think of a good habit you have. How did you build it?
Aristotle says courage sits between being reckless and being a coward. Can you think of another good trait that sits between two extremes?
Why does it help to have a friend, like Mr. Knightley, who will tell you your faults?
Kant says a good will matters most. Can someone mean well and still do harm?

comedy.question: What makes us laugh, and what is laughter for? Can comedy make people better?

stops.text: Aristophanes wrote wild comedies full of jokes, singing frogs and flying beetles. He made fun of politicians, philosophers and poets by name. Behind the laughter, he gave Athens advice about peace and good sense.

quote.text: Brekekekex, ko-ax, ko-ax! / Brekekekex, ko-ax, ko-ax!
quote.author: Aristophanes
quote.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 8, P. F. Collier and Son

stops.text: Aristotle says comedy shows people as worse than average, but in ways that are laughable rather than painful or harmful. A comic mask is ugly and twisted but causes no pain. His book on comedy is lost, but this short definition shaped later thinking.

Chaucer's pilgrims tell all kinds of tales, from noble romances to rowdy jokes. He laughs at a greedy pardoner and a vain monk with sly, gentle humor. Some tales are rude, so families usually read selections.

Erasmus lets Folly herself give a speech praising foolishness. She mocks proud scholars, greedy officials and quarreling theologians. The joke turns serious at the end, praising the holy 'foolishness' of simple faith.

Rabelais tells the adventures of giant kings with huge appetites and huge learning. His comedy is loud, silly and sometimes rude, but it mocks bad schools and stuffy officials. He says laughter is part of being human.

quote.text: Because to laugh is proper to the man.
quote.author: Rabelais
quote.ed: Book I, London

stops.text: In Shakespeare's comedies, lovers get mixed up, people wear disguises and fairies play tricks, but everything ends in marriage and celebration. The mischievous fairy Puck laughs at human foolishness. The plays are funny and also wise about love.

quote.text: Lord, what fools these mortals be!
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.work: A Midsummer Night's Dream, Act III, scene 2 (Puck)
quote.ed: First printed in the First Folio

stops.text: Molière laughs at hypocrites, misers, snobs and people who think they are sick. In The Miser, Harpagon loves his money more than his children. Molière believed comedy could correct faults by making them ridiculous.

quote.text: We must eat to live, and not live to eat.
quote.author: Molière
quote.work: The Miser, Act III, Scene V
quote.ed: The Dramatic Works of Molière, George Bell & Sons

stops.text: Swift's satire is sharper. Lilliputians go to war over which end to break an egg; scientists try to get sunlight out of cucumbers. He laughs to show how silly and proud people can be.

Voltaire's Candide rushes from disaster to disaster while his teacher Pangloss insists all is for the best. The comedy is fast and biting. It makes readers laugh and then think hard about suffering and false comfort.

Austen's comedy is quiet: misunderstandings, matchmaking gone wrong and silly neighbors who talk too much. Emma's mistakes are funny because we see them coming. In the end the comedy teaches her, and us, to see more clearly.

young: Comedy is the art of making people laugh. Funny stories often have mix-ups, silly characters and happy endings.

Some comedy is just for fun, like a joke about a frog. Other comedy, called satire, pokes fun at people being proud or greedy, to help everyone see how silly it is. Write a funny short scene where two characters get mixed up!
talk: What makes you laugh the hardest?
Rabelais says laughing is part of being human. Do animals laugh?
Is it okay to make fun of someone? When is it kind and when is it not?
Molière said comedy can fix bad habits. How?
What is the funniest story you know?

courage.question: What is courage? Is it having no fear, or doing what is right in spite of fear?

stops.text: In the Iliad, Hector knows that Achilles is stronger, and his family begs him to stay inside the walls of Troy. He goes out to face Achilles anyway, for the sake of his city and his honor. Homer shows courage mixed with fear: at first Hector even runs, then turns and stands.

At his trial, Socrates refuses to beg or to stop doing philosophy, even to save his life. He compares himself to a soldier who must not leave his post. A good person, he says, should ask only whether an act is right or wrong, not whether it brings danger.

In the Laches, two Athenian generals try to define courage and fail. One says courage is standing firm in battle, but Socrates points out courage in sickness, poverty and the sea as well. They wonder whether courage is a kind of wisdom about what is truly worth fearing, and the dialogue ends without a final answer.

Aristotle places courage between two faults: rashness, which fears too little, and cowardice, which fears too much. The brave person feels fear but faces it for a good reason and in the right way. Courage is a habit built by facing small fears first.

On the Pequod, first mate Starbuck is brave but sensible. He wants men in his boat who respect the danger of a whale, because fearless men are reckless. Melville sets his steady courage against Captain Ahab's wild daring.

quote.text: "I will have no man in my boat," said Starbuck, "who is not afraid of a whale."
quote.author: Melville
quote.ed: Harper and Brothers, New York (first American edition)

stops.text: Huck's bravest moment is not a fight. He has written a letter that would send Jim back into slavery, and everything he has been taught says sending it is right. He tears it up, ready to take the blame, because he will not betray his friend.

quote.text: I was a-trembling, because I'd got to decide, forever, betwixt two things, and I knowed it.
quote.author: Twain
quote.work: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, Chapter XXXI
quote.ed: Charles L. Webster and Company, New York

stops.text: Shaw's play shows Joan of Arc, a farm girl who leads armies and stands up to bishops and nobles. In the play she will not deny the voices she believes guide her, even at the cost of her life. Shaw presents her courage as coming from faith, plain good sense and a refusal to give in.

young: Courage doesn't mean you aren't scared. It means you do the right thing even when you are scared. A firefighter going into a burning house feels fear but goes in to help.

There is everyday courage too: telling the truth when you might get in trouble, standing up for a kid who is being teased, or trying something new at school. Huck Finn was brave because he stood by his friend when it was hard.
talk: Is someone who feels no fear brave, or just reckless? What does Starbuck think?
Can you think of a time when telling the truth took courage?
Socrates and Joan would not take back what they believed. When is it brave to stand firm, and when is it wiser to change your mind?
Aristotle says courage grows by practice. What is a small brave thing you could practice?
Who is someone you think is brave? What did they do?

dialogue.question: Why learn by talking things through? How can a conversation, even with books from long ago, lead to the truth?

stops.text: Socrates meets Euthyphro, who is sure he knows what holiness is. By asking questions, Socrates shows that Euthyphro's answers don't hold together. The conversation ends without an answer, but both now know the question better.

quote.text: The point which I should first wish to understand is whether the pious or holy is beloved by the gods because it is holy, or holy because it is beloved of the gods.
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Socrates calls himself a midwife of ideas. He doesn't give birth to his own answers, he says, but helps others bring theirs out and test whether they are sound. Philosophy begins in wonder and grows in talk.

quote.text: I see, my dear Theaetetus, that Theodorus had a true insight into your nature when he said that you were a philosopher, for wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. IV, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Aquinas's Summa is built like a debate. Each article raises objections, gives the other side, then an answer, then replies. It records the conversations of the medieval university, where students argued questions out loud.

Galileo writes as a conversation among three friends: one speaks for the new science, one for Aristotle, and one is a sharp, open-minded listener. The dialogue lets readers follow the reasoning and the objections. It makes science a shared search.

Diderot writes a lively conversation between a sober philosopher and a clever, shameless musician in a Paris café. The nephew mocks every virtue, and the philosopher struggles to answer him. Diderot never says who wins.

Boswell spent years writing down Samuel Johnson's conversation: his jokes, arguments and wise sayings. Johnson loved to talk and often argued the other side just to test an idea. The book shows how much a mind can come alive in conversation.

quote.text: Is not a Patron, my Lord, one who looks with unconcern on a man struggling for life in the water, and, when he has reached ground, encumbers him with help?
quote.author: James Boswell
quote.work: Life of Johnson: Johnson's letter to Lord Chesterfield, February 1755
quote.ed: Boswell's Life of Johnson, edited by George Birkbeck Hill, vol. I, Clarendon Press, Oxford (Project Gutenberg text)

stops.text: Niels Bohr describes his long friendly debates with Albert Einstein about quantum physics. Einstein kept proposing puzzles; Bohr kept answering them. Neither fully convinced the other, but the arguments sharpened physics for both.

The editors of Great Books of the Western World described the books as a great conversation across the centuries, each author answering earlier ones. Our opening rung tells that story and its critics. These Great Ideas pages try to let you hear that conversation.

young: A dialogue is a conversation where people share ideas, ask questions and listen. Talking things through can help us understand things better than thinking alone.
Socrates learned by asking friends questions like 'What is courage?' Try it at dinner: pick a big question, and take turns sharing ideas. Listen carefully and ask 'Why do you think that?'
talk: What is a good question to talk about at dinner?
Socrates called himself a midwife of ideas. What did he mean?
Why is listening just as important as talking?
Johnson sometimes argued the other side on purpose. Why might that help?
How can you have a conversation with a writer who lived long ago?

pages.title: Debate: argue both sides of a question

doubt.question: How much can we be sure of? Is doubt a danger, or the first step toward knowing?

stops.text: At his trial Socrates explains that the oracle at Delphi called him the wisest man in Athens. Puzzled, he questioned people famous for wisdom and found they didn't know what they thought they knew. His only wisdom, he concluded, was knowing that he did not know.

Montaigne took as his motto the question 'What do I know?' He piles up examples of how customs, opinions and even the senses differ from place to place. His doubt makes him modest and tolerant, and he still lives and writes with great enjoyment.

Hamlet doubts the ghost, his mother, his friends and himself. He stages a play to test whether his uncle is guilty. Shakespeare shows doubt as both a mark of a thoughtful mind and a trap that can freeze a person from acting.

Bacon says hasty certainty is the enemy of learning. If we start with certainties we end in doubts, but if we are willing to start with doubts, careful inquiry can lead to certainty. Doubt, used well, is a tool.

quote.text: So it is in contemplation: if a man will begin with certainties, he shall end in doubts; but if he will be content to begin with doubts, he shall end in certainties.
quote.author: Francis Bacon
quote.work: The Advancement of Learning, First Book, V.8
quote.ed: ed. Henry Morley, Cassell's National Library, Cassell & Company

stops.text: Descartes doubts on purpose, as far as doubt can go. He imagines a powerful deceiver making him wrong about everything. Yet even then, he says, he must exist in order to be deceived, and that certainty becomes his starting point.

quote.text: I will suppose, then, not that Deity, who is sovereignly good and the fountain of truth, but that some malignant demon, who is at once exceedingly potent and deceitful, has employed all his artifice to deceive me…
quote.author: René Descartes
quote.ed: Descartes' Meditations and Selections from the Principles of Philosophy, Open Court

stops.text: Hume finds that we cannot prove by reason that the future will be like the past, or even see causes at work. But he does not think we should doubt everything. Nature makes us go on believing, and he recommends a mild, modest doubt that keeps us careful.

Poincaré warns against two lazy habits: doubting everything and believing everything. Both, he says, save us the trouble of thinking. Science needs careful judgment about which parts of a theory are facts, which are conventions and which are guesses.

quote.text: To doubt everything or to believe everything are two equally convenient solutions; both dispense with the necessity of reflection.
quote.author: Henri Poincaré
quote.ed: Walter Scott Publishing

stops.text: Russell starts with a table: it looks different from every angle and in every light, so what is the real table? Philosophy may not settle such questions, he says, but it frees us from the tyranny of custom and widens our sense of what is possible.

quote.text: Is there any knowledge in the world which is so certain that no reasonable man could doubt it?
quote.author: Bertrand Russell
quote.work: The Problems of Philosophy, Chapter I
quote.ed: Williams and Norgate, London (Home University Library)

young: To doubt is to wonder if something is really true. It's good to doubt a little. If a stranger online says a magic pill will make you fly, you should doubt it!
But you can't doubt everything, or you'd never do anything. Good thinkers ask questions, check the evidence and then decide. Socrates said the first step to being wise is knowing what you don't know.
talk: What is something you used to believe and now doubt?
Socrates said he was wise because he knew he didn't know. What did he mean?
Is there anything you are completely sure of? How do you know?
When does doubting help you? When does it get in the way?
Poincaré says believing everything and doubting everything are both lazy. Do you agree?

duty.question: What do we owe to others, to our country and to God? And how do we know what we ought to do?

stops.text: Antigone's brother has died fighting against his own city, and King Creon forbids anyone to bury him. Antigone buries him anyway. She says there are unwritten laws from the gods that no ruler can cancel, and Sophocles lets both her duty to family and Creon's duty to the city speak strongly.

quote.text: Nor did I think that your decrees were of such force, that a mortal could override the unwritten and unfailing statutes given us by the gods.
quote.author: Sophocles
quote.ed: Cambridge University Press

stops.text: In prison, Socrates' friend Crito begs him to escape. Socrates refuses. He imagines the laws of Athens speaking to him: he has lived under them all his life, so breaking them now would be a wrong, and he holds that one must never do wrong, even in return for a wrong.

quote.text: that not life, but a good life, is to be chiefly valued?
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Aeneas is famous for pietas: duty to his father, his son, his people and the gods. He carries his old father out of burning Troy on his shoulders. Later he leaves Queen Dido, whom he loves, because the gods call him to found a new home in Italy, and Virgil makes us feel the cost.

quote.text: Whate’er befalls, your life shall be my care;
quote.author: Virgil
quote.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 13, P. F. Collier & Son

stops.text: The emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote notes to himself about doing his work well. Each morning he reminds himself that he will meet rude and ungrateful people, but that they are his kin and he must not be angry. People are made to work together, he says, as hands and feet do.

quote.text: For we are made for co-operation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth.
quote.author: Marcus Aurelius
quote.ed: The Chesterfield Society, London and New York

stops.text: Hamlet's father's ghost tells him to avenge a murder. Hamlet is unsure: is the ghost telling the truth, and is revenge right? The play shows a young man torn between a duty laid on him and his own doubts and conscience.

quote.text: O cursed spite, That ever I was born to set it right.
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.ed: First printed in quarto

stops.text: Kant argues that a duty binds everyone, whatever they happen to want. His test: act only on a rule you could will everyone to follow. He adds that we must treat every person as an end, never merely as a tool.

quote.text: Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a universal law.
quote.author: Immanuel Kant
quote.ed: Kant's Critique of Practical Reason and Other Works on the Theory of Ethics, 4th edition, Longmans, Green, London

stops.text: Kierkegaard retells the Bible story of Abraham, asked by God to give up his son Isaac. He asks whether a duty to God could ever stand above ordinary moral duty. He does not make it easy: he says he admires Abraham's faith but cannot understand it, and he wants readers to feel how hard the question is.

Huck's conscience, trained by his society, tells him it is his duty to turn Jim in. His heart tells him to protect his friend. Twain shows that conscience can be taught wrong, and Huck chooses the better way while believing he is doing wrong.

young: A duty is something you ought to do, even if you don't feel like it. Feeding your pet, helping at home and keeping a promise are duties.

Sometimes duties pull in different directions. Should you keep a secret for a friend, or tell a grown-up because your friend might get hurt? The great books are full of people trying to find the right thing to do when two duties clash.
talk: What duties do you have at home? At school?
Antigone chose her family over the king's law. Was she right? What would Creon say?
Kant says: only do what you would be okay with everyone doing. Try his test on telling a small lie.
Huck's conscience told him the wrong thing. How can we tell if our conscience is right?
Can a promise ever be broken for a good reason?

education.question: What is education for, and how do people really learn?

stops.text: Socrates asks an enslaved boy questions about a square, without telling him the answer. Step by step the boy discovers how to double the square's area. Socrates says learning is drawing out what is already in the soul, and Plato calls it recollection.

Plato says education is not putting sight into blind eyes but turning the whole person toward the light. He lays out years of study, from music and gymnastics to mathematics and philosophy. The goal is people who can see the good and rule wisely.

Augustine was a teacher of speaking before he became a bishop. He advises Christian teachers to use the skills of good speakers: to teach clearly, to delight so listeners keep listening, and to move them to act. He also tells students to learn useful arts and sciences wherever they are found.

quote.text: “To teach is a necessity, to delight is a beauty, to persuade is a triumph.”
quote.author: Augustine
quote.work: On Christian Doctrine, Book IV, chapter 12
quote.ed: A Select Library of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, vol. II, The Christian Literature Company, Buffalo

stops.text: Rabelais mocks old-fashioned schooling, where the giant Gargantua memorizes books backward and learns nothing. His new tutor fills the day with reading, talks on walks, games, music, science and looking at the stars. It is comedy, but it carries a real hope for a fuller education.

Montaigne says a child's head should be well made rather than well filled. A good teacher lets the student judge, question and put lessons into practice. Students should digest what they learn the way bees turn flowers into their own honey.

quote.text: Bees cull their several sweets from this flower and that blossom, here and there where they find them, but themselves afterward make the honey, which is all and purely their own, and no more thyme and marjoram ...
quote.author: Montaigne
quote.work: Essays, Book I, Chapter 25, "Of the Education of Children"
quote.tr: Charles Cotton, revised by William Carew Hazlitt
quote.ed: Reeves and Turner, London

stops.text: Bacon defends learning against those who say it makes people proud or useless. He surveys all the branches of knowledge to show what is known and what still needs work. Learning, he argues, should serve both the mind and the good of all.

William James, who taught teachers as well as students, explains how attention and habit work. You can't learn what you don't attend to, and attention wanders. Good teaching connects new things to what the student already cares about.

quote.text: Every one knows what attention is.
quote.author: William James
quote.work: The Principles of Psychology, Chapter XI (Attention)
quote.ed: Henry Holt and Company, New York

stops.text: Joyce follows Stephen Dedalus from a small boy at school to a young man choosing his own path. His strict schooling gives him great learning, and he ends by setting out to shape his life as an artist. The novel's style grows up as Stephen does.

John Dewey, a leader of new kinds of schools, warns against both old drill and careless freedom. Real education, he says, comes from experiences that lead to further growth, chosen and guided by a thoughtful teacher. Learning by doing must still be learning.

young: Education means learning. You learn at school, but also at home, outside, from books and by trying things yourself.

Socrates taught by asking questions instead of giving answers, so his students figured things out for themselves. Montaigne said learning should be like bees making honey: you gather from many flowers and make something that's your own. Try teaching someone a game by only asking questions!
talk: What is the best thing you've ever learned? How did you learn it?
Socrates taught by asking questions. Is that a good way to learn? Why?
Montaigne says a well-made head is better than a full one. What do you think he meant?
What makes a teacher great?
What do you want to learn next?

electricity.question: What are magnetism and electricity, and how did people find out they are connected?

stops.text: Lucretius tries to explain the magnet, a stone that pulls iron, using atoms. He suggests that streams of atoms flowing from the stone clear a space, and iron atoms rush in. The explanation was wrong, but it treated magnetism as natural, not magic.

Galen uses the lodestone as a comparison. Just as the stone draws iron, he argues, the organs of the body draw to themselves what they need. He believed living bodies have attractive powers like the magnet's.

quote.text: It has to do with the famous and far-renowned stone which draws iron [the lodestone].
quote.author: Galen
quote.work: On the Natural Faculties, Book I, 14
quote.ed: Loeb Classical Library, Heinemann and Putnam

stops.text: Gilbert tested old claims with experiments, and threw out myths such as that garlic stops a magnet. Using a small round magnet as a model, he showed the earth itself is a great magnet, which is why compasses point north. He also studied how rubbed amber attracts things, and his Latin word electricus gave English the word electric.

quote.text: Hence some suspect that garlick is of avail against any deleterious power of the magnet: thus in philosophy many false and idle conjectures arise from fables and falsehoods.
quote.author: William Gilbert
quote.work: On the Magnet, Book I, chapter 14
quote.tr: Silvanus P. Thompson and the Gilbert Club
quote.ed: Chiswick Press, London

stops.text: Faraday discovers that a changing magnetic field makes electric current flow in a wire. He pictures lines of force filling the space around magnets and currents. His discoveries are the basis of the electric generator and transformer.

quote.text: When the contact was made, there was a sudden and very slight effect at the galvanometer, and there was also a similar slight effect when the contact with the battery was broken.
quote.author: Michael Faraday
quote.work: Experimental Researches in Electricity, First Series, paragraph 10
quote.ed: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, vol. 122

stops.text: Einstein's relativity grew partly from a puzzle in electricity and magnetism. Moving a magnet near a wire or a wire near a magnet gives the same current, yet the old theory described the two cases differently. Relativity shows that electricity and magnetism are two sides of one thing.

young: Magnets pull on iron and stick to the fridge. A compass needle is a little magnet that points north, because the whole earth is a giant magnet! William Gilbert figured that out over 400 years ago.
Electricity is what lights your lamps. Michael Faraday found that moving a magnet near a coil of wire makes electricity. That's how power stations make electricity today: spinning magnets and wires.
talk: Rub a balloon on your hair. What happens when you hold it near small bits of paper?
Gilbert tested whether garlic stops a magnet. Why was it important to test old claims?
How does a compass work?
What things in your home use electricity? What would life be like without it?

equality.question: In what ways are people equal? And what follows from it for laws, families and governments?

stops.text: Aristotle says justice means treating equals equally and unequals unequally, so everything depends on who counts as equal. He reports that democrats think free birth makes people equal, while oligarchs think wealth makes them unequal. He also held that some people are slaves by nature, a view that later thinkers rejected.

Hobbes argues that nature made people roughly equal in body and mind. Even the weakest can kill the strongest by trickery or by joining with others. This equality, he says, breeds fear and rivalry, which is why people need a government.

Locke holds that in the state of nature all people are equal and independent, with no one born to rule another. Political power can therefore rest only on consent. His argument became one of the foundations for later talk of equal rights.

quote.text: Men being, as has been said, by nature all free, equal, and independent, no one can be put out of this estate and subjected to the political power of another without his own consent…
quote.author: John Locke
quote.ed: Two Treatises on Civil Government, Morley's Universal Library, 2nd edition, George Routledge and Sons, London

stops.text: Rousseau separates natural inequality, such as strength or age, from inequality that society creates, such as wealth and rank. He traces the second kind to the rise of private property. His story of how it began is one of the most famous openings in political writing.

quote.text: The first man who, having enclosed a piece of ground, bethought himself of saying This is mine, and found people simple enough to believe him, was the real founder of civil society.
quote.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
quote.work: Discourse on the Origin of Inequality, Part II
quote.ed: The Social Contract & Discourses, Everyman's Library, J. M. Dent, London, and E. P. Dutton, New York

stops.text: The Declaration of Independence states that all men are created equal and given rights by their Creator. Its signers did not end slavery, and that gap was argued over from the start. Later Americans, including those who worked to end slavery and to win votes for women, appealed to these same words.

Visiting the United States, Tocqueville is struck most by the equality of conditions: no nobles, and people in every rank meeting as equals. He thinks equality is spreading everywhere. He admires much of it, but warns that a love of equality can sometimes outweigh a love of liberty.

quote.text: Amongst the novel objects that attracted my attention during my stay in the United States, nothing struck me more forcibly than the general equality of conditions.
quote.author: Tocqueville
quote.ed: Colonial Press, New York (revised edition)

stops.text: In A Doll's House, Nora's husband treats her like a pet. When she finally sees it, she leaves to learn who she is. Ibsen's play started arguments across Europe about equality in marriage, and he leaves the audience to judge.

quote.text: I think that before all else I am a human being, just as much as you are—or at least I will try to become one.
quote.author: Ibsen
quote.ed: Ibsen's Prose Dramas, ed. William Archer (Walter Scott, London)

stops.text: In Orwell's fable, farm animals overthrow their farmer in the name of equality. Little by little the pigs take power, change the rules and live like the old masters. Orwell shows how the words of equality can be twisted by those who want power.

young: Equal means the same in some important way. You and your friends may not be equally tall or equally fast, but you are equally people, and you each deserve to be treated fairly.
In a race, everyone starts at the same line: that's equal. But should the youngest kid get a head start? People argue about which kinds of equality matter most, and the great books argue too.
talk: In what ways are you and your best friend different? In what ways are you equal?
Is it fair to treat everyone exactly the same? When might it not be?
The Declaration said all men are created equal, but slavery went on. How did later people use those words?
In Animal Farm the pigs change the rules. Why is it important that rules apply to everyone?

evil.question: Why is there evil and suffering in the world? Where does wrongdoing come from?

stops.text: Socrates argues that doing wrong is worse than suffering it, because it damages the wrongdoer's own soul. He also holds that no one does wrong willingly; evil comes from ignorance of what is truly good. His listeners find this hard to believe.

Augustine argues that evil is not a thing God made but the lack or twisting of something good, like sickness in a body. Moral evil comes from free wills turning away from God toward lesser goods. God, he says, can bring good even out of evil.
Aquinas faces the objection that if God is all good and all powerful, there should be no evil. He answers, following Augustine, that God permits evil only because he can bring a greater good from it.

quote.text: Since God is the highest good, He would not allow any evil to exist in His works, unless His omnipotence and goodness were such as to bring good even out of evil.
quote.author: Thomas Aquinas
quote.work: Summa Theologica, First Part, Question 2, Article 3, Reply to Objection 1 (quoting Augustine)
quote.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province
quote.ed: Second and Revised Edition

stops.text: Dante's Hell is arranged by kinds of wrongdoing, from weakness to violence to fraud, which he thought worst because it misuses reason. Each punishment fits the sin. The journey through Hell is the first stage of a pilgrim's return to the good.

Macbeth shows evil growing in a good man, step by step. The witches tempt him, his wife urges him, but he chooses. Once he starts, each crime leads to the next, until his life seems to him to mean nothing.

quote.text: Fair is foul, and foul is fair:
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.ed: First printed in the First Folio

stops.text: Milton tells of Satan's rebellion and the fall of Adam and Eve. He sets out to show that God is just in allowing evil, because creatures made free must be able to choose wrongly. Many readers find Satan the most vivid character, which has fueled centuries of argument.

quote.text: That, to the height of this great argument, I may assert Eternal Providence, And justify the ways of God to men.
quote.author: John Milton
quote.ed: 2nd edition, S. Simmons, London; Project Gutenberg text

stops.text: After a great earthquake destroyed Lisbon in 1755, Voltaire wrote Candide to mock the claim that this is the best of all possible worlds. His characters suffer one disaster after another while Dr. Pangloss explains it is all for the best. Voltaire's answer is practical: stop theorizing and tend your garden.

quote.text: He proved admirably that there is no effect without a cause, and that, in this best of all possible worlds, the Baron's castle was the most magnificent of castles, and his lady the best of all possible Baronesses.
quote.author: Voltaire
quote.ed: Candide, The Modern Library, Boni and Liveright, New York

stops.text: Goethe's devil, Mephistopheles, calls himself part of the power that always wants evil and always ends up doing good. Faust makes a bargain with him, and wrong follows. Goethe suggests that striving and love can still win out over evil.

quote.text: Part of that Power, not understood, Which always wills the Bad, and always works the Good.
quote.author: Goethe
quote.ed: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, Boston (1882 printing)

stops.text: Ivan Karamazov lists true stories of cruelty to children and says no future harmony could justify them. It is one of the strongest statements of the problem of evil ever written. Dostoevsky, a Christian, answers through the elder Zosima's teaching of active, forgiving love.

Marlow travels up an African river to find Kurtz, a European trader who has given in to greed and power. Conrad suggests that the darkness lies not in a place but in the human heart, and in the greed of the empire Marlow serves. The story has mature themes, best for older readers.

young: Evil means something very bad, like being cruel or hurting people on purpose. Suffering means being hurt, sad or sick. People have always asked: why do bad things happen?

Some writers say people choose wrong when they forget what is truly good. Others say suffering can lead to something good, the way a hard time can make us stronger or kinder. Voltaire said: stop arguing and help make the world better, like tending a garden.
talk: Why do you think people sometimes choose to do wrong?
Socrates says doing wrong hurts the wrongdoer most. How could that be?
Macbeth's first wrong choice led to more. Why does one bad choice make the next easier?
Voltaire says 'tend your garden.' What could you do to make things better around you?
Can something good ever come from something bad? Share an example.

evolution.question: Have living things always been the way they are, or have they changed over long ages? How?

stops.text: Aristotle reports an older idea from Empedocles: that long ago animals came together by chance, and only the well-fitted ones survived. He rejects it. Living things, he argues, grow according to purpose, since their parts are too regularly fitted to be mere chance.

Lucretius writes that the earth once produced many strange creatures, and those that could not feed, defend themselves and have young died out. It is not evolution as Darwin meant it, since species did not change into new ones, but it is an early idea of nature weeding out the unfit.

Darwin gathers evidence from breeders, fossils, islands and the shapes of living things. He argues that species change over many generations by natural selection: helpful variations are kept, harmful ones lost. He admitted gaps in the evidence and answered objections at length.

quote.text: This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection.
quote.author: Darwin
quote.work: On the Origin of Species, Chapter IV
quote.ed: John Murray, London (first edition)

stops.text: Darwin applies his theory to human beings, arguing that people share ancestors with other animals. He spends much of the book on how moral sense and kindness could develop. He calls conscience the most important difference between humans and other animals.

quote.text: I fully subscribe to the judgment of those writers who maintain that of all the differences between man and the lower animals, the moral sense or conscience is by far the most important. ...
quote.author: Darwin
quote.work: The Descent of Man, Chapter IV
quote.ed: John Murray, London (first edition)

stops.text: Dobzhansky joins Darwin's theory with the new science of genes. He shows how variation, inheritance and selection work in wild populations, especially fruit flies. His book helped build what is called the modern synthesis.

Waddington asks how development and evolution fit together. Changes in how an embryo grows, he argues, are what natural selection works on. He wanted biology to explain both the history of life and the growth of each living thing.

young: Long ago there were dinosaurs, giant ferns and woolly mammoths. Today there are different animals. Charles Darwin studied how living things change over very long times.

He noticed that animals have babies that are a little different from each other. The ones best suited to their home, like a bird whose beak fits the seeds nearby, tend to survive and have more babies. Over many, many generations, that adds up to big changes. People hold different beliefs about how this fits with faith, and families can talk about that together.
talk: Look at pictures of dogs of different breeds. How did people make them so different?
Why might a white rabbit survive better in snowy places?
Darwin said conscience was the most important difference between people and animals. What do you think?
How do fossils help us learn about the past?

experience.question: What can our senses teach us, and what can't they? Do we see the world as it really is?

stops.text: The young mathematician Theaetetus suggests that knowledge is simply perception. Socrates tests the idea: the same wind feels cold to one person and warm to another, and we judge things the senses alone cannot, such as sameness and difference. So knowing must be more than sensing.

quote.text: I see, my dear Theaetetus, that Theodorus had a true insight into your nature when he said that you were a philosopher, for wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. IV, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Aristotle explains that a sense takes in the form of a thing without its matter, as wax takes the shape of a signet ring without the metal. Each sense has its own objects, like color for sight and sound for hearing. He trusted the senses as our starting point for knowing nature.

Locke traces all ideas to experience. He separates qualities like size and shape, which he thought are really in things, from qualities like color and taste, which arise in us. His question of how far our ideas copy the world set the agenda for the next century.

quote.text: Let us then suppose the mind to be, as we say, white paper, void of all characters, without any ideas; how comes it to be furnished?
quote.author: John Locke
quote.ed: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Thomas Tegg, London

stops.text: Newton's prism experiments show that white sunlight is a mix of rays bent by different amounts. He adds a careful remark: the rays themselves are not colored. Color is the sensation they stir up in us.

quote.text: For the Rays to speak properly are not coloured.
quote.author: Isaac Newton
quote.work: Opticks, Book I, Part II, Proposition II, Definition
quote.ed: 4th edition, William Innys, London

stops.text: Berkeley argues that if color and taste exist only in the mind, so must shape and size, since we never meet one without the other. Things exist as perceived. He believed this answered doubt, since the world we see is the real world, kept in being by God.

quote.text: Their ESSE is PERCIPI, nor is it possible they should have any existence out of the minds or thinking things which perceive them.
quote.author: George Berkeley
quote.ed: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710), Project Gutenberg text

stops.text: Hume says that all our ideas are copies of impressions from the senses or feelings. When a word stands for no impression at all, we should be suspicious of it. Experience is our only guide to matters of fact, and it works by habit.

Kant agrees that knowledge begins with experience but says the mind gives experience its shape. We see the world in space and time and as linked by causes because that is how our minds must take it in. What things are in themselves, apart from us, we cannot know.

quote.text: That all our knowledge begins with experience there can be no doubt. … But, though all our knowledge begins with experience, it by no means follows that all arises out of experience.
quote.author: Immanuel Kant
quote.ed: Critique of Pure Reason, Bohn's Philosophical Library (Project Gutenberg text)

stops.text: William James studies experience as a scientist of the mind. He notices that we never get pure sensations; experience flows like a stream, and attention picks out what we notice. What we see depends partly on what we are ready to see.

quote.text: Consciousness, then, does not appear to itself chopped up in bits.
quote.author: William James
quote.work: The Principles of Psychology, Chapter IX (The Stream of Thought)
quote.ed: Henry Holt and Company, New York

young: Your five senses are how you meet the world: seeing, hearing, touching, tasting and smelling. They teach you a lot! But they can be fooled. A straw in a glass of water looks bent, but it isn't.

Here's a puzzle the great thinkers loved: is a strawberry red when no one is looking? Newton said light rays aren't really colored; the color happens when light meets our eyes and brain. Try it: what color is your room in the dark?
talk: Can you think of a time your eyes or ears fooled you?
Is the strawberry red when no one is looking? What would Newton say? What would Berkeley say?
Put one hand in warm water and one in cold, then both in lukewarm water. What happens? What does that tell you about your senses?
What do you notice when you pay close attention that you usually miss?

experiment.question: Why test ideas instead of only arguing about them? How did people learn to ask nature questions with experiments?

stops.text: Aristotle was a great observer. He opened eggs day by day to watch chicks grow and gathered reports from fishermen and farmers. He did not do controlled experiments as we know them, but he insisted on checking theory against what we see.

Galen did real experiments. To show that the kidneys make urine, he tied the tubes leading from them to the bladder in a living animal and watched what happened. He scolded rivals who argued without testing.

Gilbert says the old books are full of untested claims about magnets. He tests them himself, rubbing magnets with garlic and showing nothing changes. He calls for true experiments in place of guesses and fables.

quote.text: Plutarch and Claudius Ptolemy, and all the copyists since their time, think that a loadstone smeared with garlick does not allure iron.
quote.author: William Gilbert
quote.work: On the Magnet, Book I, chapter 14
quote.tr: Silvanus P. Thompson and the Gilbert Club
quote.ed: Chiswick Press, London

stops.text: Bacon argues that knowledge grows by planned experiments and careful tables of cases, not by clever argument alone. He warns that we notice cases that fit our ideas and forget the ones that don't. Experiments should be designed to catch our mistakes.

quote.text: The former like ants only heap up and use their store, the latter like spiders spin out their own webs.
quote.author: Francis Bacon
quote.tr: the version edited by Joseph Devey
quote.ed: P. F. Collier & Son, New York

stops.text: Harvey ties tight and loose bands on an arm to show which way blood flows in arteries and veins. He presses on veins to show the valves only let blood go toward the heart. Simple experiments anyone could repeat made his case.

Galileo rolls balls down a smooth grooved ramp many times and times them carefully. He repeats the test at different slopes and finds the same law. An experiment, for him, is a question asked of nature in the language of mathematics.

Pascal designs experiments with tubes of mercury and water to test whether nature abhors a vacuum. The test on a mountain shows the air's weight holds up the mercury. He says the ancients would have changed their minds if they had seen it.

quote.text: But if the modern experiments had been known to them, perhaps they would have found cause for affirming what they found cause for denying, for the reason that vacuum had not yet appeared.
quote.author: Blaise Pascal
quote.work: Preface to the Treatise on Vacuum
quote.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 48, P. F. Collier and Son

stops.text: Newton passes sunlight through one prism, picks out a single color, and sends it through a second prism. The color bends again but does not change. This crucial experiment showed that colors are in the light, not made by the glass.

quote.text: The Light of the Sun consists of Rays differently Refrangible.
quote.author: Isaac Newton
quote.work: Opticks, Book I, Part I, Proposition II, Theorem II, Experiment 3
quote.ed: 4th edition, William Innys, London

stops.text: Faraday kept careful numbered notes of thousands of experiments. After many failures, he found that a current appears only when a magnet moves or a current switches on or off. He wrote his results so clearly that others could repeat them.

quote.text: But whilst the voltaic current was continuing to pass through the one helix, no galvanometrical appearances of any effect like induction upon the other helix could be perceived.
quote.author: Michael Faraday
quote.work: Experimental Researches in Electricity, First Series, paragraph 10
quote.ed: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, vol. 122

young: An experiment is a test to find out if an idea is true. Instead of just saying 'I think heavy things fall faster,' you drop two things and watch!
A good experiment changes only one thing at a time. Want to know if plants need light? Grow two bean plants the same way, but put one in a dark closet. What happens after a week?
talk: Why is it better to test an idea than just argue about it?
Gilbert tested whether garlic stops magnets. Can you test an old saying, like 'a watched pot never boils'?
Why should an experiment change only one thing at a time?
Faraday kept careful notes. Why do scientists write everything down?
Plan an experiment together. What will you change, and what will you measure?

facing-death.question: How should we think about death? Should we fear it, and how does it change the way we live?

stops.text: Achilles knows he can have a long quiet life at home or a short life with lasting glory. He chooses glory. Homer shows the warriors facing death with courage but also with grief, and the poem ends with two enemies, Achilles and old King Priam, weeping together over their losses.

On the last day of his life, Socrates talks calmly with his friends about the soul. He argues that the soul lives on after death, and that philosophy, which turns the mind from the body to the truth, is a lifelong practice for dying. He dies peacefully, and Plato calls him the wisest and best man he knew.

quote.text: And the true philosophers, Simmias, are always occupied in the practice of dying, wherefore also to them least of all men is death terrible.
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Lucretius gives the opposite reason not to fear death. Following Epicurus, he teaches that the soul is made of atoms that scatter when we die, so there is no one left to suffer. We did not mind the ages before we were born, he says, so we need not mind the ages after.

Marcus Aurelius reminds himself that death is a natural change, like ripening or growing old. Everything passes, even the famous. So he tries to live each day well, as if it might be his last, without fear or complaint.

Montaigne first writes that to do philosophy is to learn how to die, and he tries to keep death in mind. Later, after a bad fall from his horse that nearly killed him, he relaxes: nature will teach us how to die when the time comes. What matters is to live well now.

Hamlet thinks hard about death: about the skull of a jester he knew as a boy, and about what may come after. By the end he is calmer, saying that readiness is all. Shakespeare gives no single answer, but lets us watch a mind wrestle with the question.

quote.text: To be, or not to be, that is the question:
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.ed: First printed in quarto

stops.text: At the end of the novel, the old knight comes home sick and wakes up clear in mind. He gives up his knightly dreams, makes his will and makes his peace. His squire Sancho, weeping, begs him to get up and go adventuring again.

quote.text: "Ah!" said Sancho weeping, "don't die, master, but take my advice and live many years; for the foolishest thing a man can do in this life is to let himself die without rhyme or reason ..."
quote.author: Cervantes
quote.work: Don Quixote, Part Two, Chapter LXXIV
quote.ed: Smith, Elder, London

young: Every living thing has a beginning and an end: flowers, pets and people too. It is normal to feel sad or scared when we think about it, and it is good to talk about those feelings with someone you love.

The great writers believed different things about what happens after death, but many agreed on one thing: knowing life doesn't last forever helps us use it well. It helps us be kind today, say thank you and spend time with the people we love.
talk: Socrates and Lucretius both said not to fear death, for opposite reasons. What were their reasons?
How might remembering that life is short change the way you spend a day?
Why do you think Achilles chose glory over a long, quiet life? Would you?
How do people in your family remember those who have died?

faith-and-reason.question: How do believing and reasoning fit together? Are they friends, rivals or partners?
faith-and-reason.intro: Each stop describes an author's own view. Thinkers of faith and thinkers of reason appear side by side, and readers can weigh them.

stances.label: Faith and reason work together
Faith reaches beyond reason
Reason as the test of belief

stops.text: Augustine encourages Christians to learn logic, history and science, since all truth belongs to God. His motto is often summed up as 'believe in order to understand': faith comes first, and then reason explores what is believed.

quote.text: Let every good and true Christian understand that wherever truth may be found, it belongs to his Master.
quote.author: Augustine
quote.work: On Christian Doctrine, Book II, chapter 18
quote.ed: A Select Library of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, vol. II, The Christian Literature Company, Buffalo

stops.text: Aquinas argues that faith and reason can't truly conflict, because both come from God. Reason can prove some things, like God's existence, while faith teaches others, like the Trinity, that are above reason but not against it. He used Aristotle's philosophy to explain Christian teaching.

Erasmus has Folly mock theologians who split hairs over questions no one can answer. He praises a simple faith and a life like Christ's over clever debate. A scholar himself, he wanted learning to serve plain goodness.

Calvin holds that human reason, damaged by sin, can't find its way to true knowledge of God alone. Scripture, he says, is like glasses that let weak eyes see clearly. Reason is a gift for earthly matters, but faith rests on God's word.

quote.text: On the other hand, it is evident that man never attains to a true self-knowledge until he have previously contemplated the face of God, and come down after such contemplation to look into himself.
quote.author: John Calvin
quote.work: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book I, Chapter 1
quote.ed: Calvin Translation Society, Edinburgh

stops.text: Pascal respects reason but says its last step is to see that many things are beyond it. The heart, he says, knows first principles and knows God in a way reason cannot prove. Faith is not against reason but goes beyond it.

quote.text: The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
quote.author: Blaise Pascal
quote.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 48, P. F. Collier & Son

stops.text: Hume argues that a wise person matches belief to evidence. In his essay on miracles, he says that the evidence of experience against a miracle will usually outweigh any report of one. Believers replied that his argument assumes what it sets out to prove.

Kierkegaard argues that faith is not a conclusion reason reaches but a leap a person makes. Using Abraham's story, he says faith goes further than anything ethics or philosophy can explain. He thought his age had made faith too easy by treating it as a matter of argument.

Barth argues that people do not climb up to God by reasoning; God speaks to them through the Bible. He was reacting against theologians who made faith fit the ideas of the day. For him, faith answers God's word rather than human arguments.

quote.text: As ministers we ought to speak of God.
quote.author: Karl Barth
quote.work: The Word of God and the Word of Man, The Word of God and the Task of the Ministry (1922)
quote.ed: The Pilgrim Press, Boston

stops.text: Whitehead, a mathematician and philosopher, argues that modern science grew from a belief, partly inherited from medieval theology, that nature is orderly and understandable. Religion and science, he says, have both changed over time, and their clashes can be a chance for each to deepen.

quote.text: My explanation is that the faith in the possibility of science, generated antecedently to the development of modern scientific theory, is an unconscious derivative from medieval theology.
quote.author: Alfred North Whitehead
quote.work: Science and the Modern World, Chapter I
quote.ed: The Macmillan Company, New York

young: Faith means trusting and believing, often in God. Reason means thinking things through, step by step. Some people think faith and reason are like two wings that help a bird fly. Others think faith goes beyond what reason can show, and some think reason should be the judge of what to believe.
You use both every day. You trust your parents when they say a stove is hot (that's a kind of faith), and you also figure out a puzzle by thinking (that's reason).
talk: What things do you believe because someone you trust told you?
Aquinas thought faith and reason can't really disagree. Pascal said the heart has reasons. What do they mean?
Can a scientist also be a person of faith? Can you think of examples from history?
How do you decide whom to trust?

family.question: What is a family for, and what do parents and children owe each other?

stops.text: Odysseus spends ten years trying to get home to his wife Penelope and son Telemachus. Penelope stays loyal, and Telemachus grows up looking for his father. When Odysseus finally arrives in disguise, his old dog Argos is the first to know him.

quote.text: As soon as he saw Ulysses standing there, he dropped his ears and wagged his tail, but he could not get close up to his master.
quote.author: Homer
quote.ed: Longmans, Green

stops.text: In his ideal city, Plato proposes that the guardians should have no private families, so they will treat the whole city as their family. It is one of his most startling ideas. Even ancient readers found it hard to accept.

Aristotle answers Plato that the family is the first natural community, out of which villages and cities grow. Sharing everything would weaken love, he argues, because what belongs to everyone is cared for by no one. A city needs real families.

Two families in Verona are locked in an old feud. Their children fall in love and marry in secret, and the hatred between the houses leads to their deaths. Only then do the parents end the feud, too late.

quote.text: Two households, both alike in dignity, In fair Verona, where we lay our scene, From ancient grudge break to new mutiny, Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean.
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.ed: First printed in quarto

stops.text: Old King Lear divides his kingdom among the daughters who flatter him most and banishes Cordelia, who loves him truly but will not flatter. The flatterers then turn on him. The play is about what children and parents owe each other, and about forgiveness that comes almost too late.

quote.text: How sharper than a serpent's tooth it is To have a thankless child!
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.work: King Lear, Act I, scene 4 (Lear, of Goneril)
quote.ed: First printed in the First Folio

stops.text: Hegel sees the family as the first place where people live in unity through love. Children are raised there to become free, independent adults. Then they leave to form families of their own.

Tolstoy follows several families through war and peace, above all the lively Rostovs. Their love, quarrels, losses and new marriages carry the story. In the end the novel finds much of life's meaning in family and home.

In A Doll's House, a family that looks happy rests on secrets and on a wife treated as a child. Ibsen asks what a marriage should be: a partnership of equals or something else. Many audiences of his day were shocked by the ending.

quote.text: Before all else you are a wife and a mother.
quote.author: Ibsen
quote.ed: Ibsen's Prose Dramas, ed. William Archer (Walter Scott, London)

stops.text: Three very different brothers, a passionate soldier, a brilliant skeptic and a gentle novice, have a selfish father. Dostoevsky asks what we owe a parent who has failed us, and what brothers owe one another. Through Alyosha, he suggests that love and good memories of childhood can save a person.

young: A family is the people who take care of you and love you. Families come in many shapes. They give us food and a home, but also love, stories and someone to come home to.
In the great stories, families quarrel, forgive and help each other. Odysseus spent ten years trying to get back to his family. Even his old dog was waiting for him!
talk: What makes your family special?
What do parents owe children? What do children owe parents?
Why do you think Cordelia wouldn't flatter her father?
Romeo and Juliet's families were fighting. How can families end a quarrel?
What is a family tradition you love?

fate.question: Are our lives fixed in advance, or are they ours to choose? Can fate and free will both be true?

stops.text: An oracle foretells that Oedipus will kill his father and marry his mother. Everyone tries to escape the prophecy, and their efforts make it come true. Yet Oedipus chooses to search out the truth and takes responsibility. Sophocles leaves fate and choice tangled together.

Aeneas is driven by fate to found Rome, and even the goddess Juno can only delay it. But he still has to choose, again and again, to follow his destiny. Virgil shows fate as a calling that takes courage to obey.

quote.text: Jove will soon dispose To future good our past and present woes. … An hour will come, with pleasure to relate Your sorrows past, as benefits of Fate.”
quote.author: Virgil
quote.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 13, P. F. Collier & Son

stops.text: Augustine rejects the idea of blind fate ruled by the stars. He argues that God knows all things in advance, yet human wills are still free, because God foreknows what we will freely choose. His answer was debated by later thinkers for centuries.

Troilus, in despair, wonders whether everything is fixed by God's foreknowledge. Chaucer drew this speech from Boethius, a Roman writer much read in the Middle Ages. The poem lets fortune's wheel turn while asking how free its people really are.

The prologue calls Romeo and Juliet star-crossed lovers, as if doomed from the start. Yet the play is full of rash choices, bad timing and a feud people could have ended. Shakespeare lets the audience wonder how much was fate.

quote.text: From forth the fatal loins of these two foes A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life;
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.ed: First printed in quarto

stops.text: Cassius tells Brutus not to blame the stars: if they are underlings, it is their own fault. It is a famous claim for free will. The play goes on to show how their choices lead to their downfall.

quote.text: The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, But in ourselves, that we are underlings.
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.ed: First printed in the First Folio

stops.text: The witches tell Macbeth he will be king. Would it have happened anyway? Macbeth chooses to murder to make it come true. The play suggests that prophecy tempts, but people choose.

Milton's God says he made angels and people free, able to stand or fall. He foresaw the fall but did not cause it. Milton's whole poem rests on the belief that freedom is real and that the choice was Adam and Eve's.

Tolstoy argues that each person feels free in each moment, yet history moves by laws made of millions of choices. Napoleon thought he steered events, but was carried by them. He tries to hold freedom and necessity together.

John Marcher is sure something huge and terrible is waiting to happen to him, like a beast in the jungle. He waits all his life, and lets his friend May's love go by unnoticed. Too late he sees that his fate was to have missed his life by waiting.

quote.text: Something or other lay in wait for him, amid the twists and the turns of the months and the years, like a crouching Beast in the Jungle.
quote.author: Henry James
quote.work: The Beast in the Jungle, chapter II
quote.ed: The Better Sort (first published 1903); text of the Martin Secker edition, London

young: Fate is the idea that some things are meant to happen, no matter what. Free will is the idea that we choose what we do.

In many old stories, heroes try to escape a prophecy, and it happens anyway! But in others, like Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, a character says our lives are up to us, not the stars. Do you think your future is already set, or do you make it?
talk: Do you think some things are meant to happen?
Cassius says 'the fault is not in our stars, but in ourselves.' What does that mean?
If Macbeth hadn't met the witches, would he still have become king?
John Marcher waited his whole life for something to happen. What lesson might that teach?
What choice did you make today that changed what happened next?

forgiveness.question: What do we do after someone does wrong? Can guilt be healed, and why forgive?

stops.text: Orestes is hunted by the Furies, spirits of revenge, for avenging his father. Athena's court acquits him, and she persuades the angry Furies to become kindly guardians of Athens. The trilogy ends not in punishment but in reconciliation.

Augustine tells the story of his own wrongdoing, starting with stealing pears as a boy just for the thrill of it. In a garden in Milan, weeping, he hears a child's voice say 'take up and read,' opens the Bible and finds peace. The whole book thanks God for forgiving him.

quote.text: Take up and read.” Instantly, my countenance altered, I began to think most intently, whether children were wont in any kind of play to sing such words: nor could I remember ever to have heard the like.
quote.author: Augustine
quote.ed: A Library of Fathers of the Holy Catholic Church, John Henry Parker, Oxford

stops.text: Dante's Purgatory is a mountain where forgiven souls are healed of their faults, one terrace at a time. Here, unlike in Hell, everyone is hopeful. Love, rightly ordered, is what they are learning.

quote.text: And of that second region will I sing, In which the human spirit from sinful blot Is purg'd, and for ascent to Heaven prepares.
quote.author: Dante
quote.ed: The Vision, London

stops.text: King Lear banished his loyal daughter Cordelia. When they meet again, broken and humbled, he kneels and asks forgiveness. She says she has no cause to blame him, one of the most moving reconciliations in drama.
Prospero has his old enemies in his power at last. Instead of revenge, he chooses forgiveness, saying that virtue is a rarer action than vengeance. Then he gives up his magic.

quote.text: Yet with my nobler reason 'gainst my fury Do I take part: the rarer action is In virtue than in vengeance: they being penitent,
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.ed: First printed in the First Folio

stops.text: Emma makes a cruel joke at Miss Bates's expense during a picnic. Mr. Knightley tells her how unkind it was, and she is ashamed. The next morning she visits Miss Bates to make amends, and Austen shows how a real apology begins to mend things.

Faust does great harm in his bargain with the devil. Yet at the end of Part Two, angels carry his soul upward, because he never stopped striving and because of love, including that of Gretchen, whom he wronged. Goethe's ending has been argued over ever since.

quote.text: Whoe'er aspires unweariedly Is not beyond redeeming.
quote.author: Goethe
quote.ed: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, Boston (1882 printing)

stops.text: The elder Zosima teaches that each person is responsible for all, and that love can forgive anything. He tells how, as a young officer, he struck his servant, then asked his forgiveness. Alyosha carries this teaching into the world.

quote.text: Love all God's creation, the whole and every grain of sand in it.
quote.author: Dostoevsky
quote.work: The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, Chapter III
quote.ed: William Heinemann, London
