young: Everyone makes mistakes. When we hurt someone, we can say sorry and try to make it right. When someone hurts us, we can choose to forgive them.

Forgiving doesn't mean pretending it didn't happen. It means letting go of wanting to get even. In Shakespeare's play The Tempest, Prospero could have taken revenge, but he chose to forgive, and everyone could start again.
talk: What makes a good apology?
Is it hard for you to forgive? Why?
Prospero says forgiveness is rarer than revenge. Why do you think it's rare?
Emma went to apologize the next morning. Why is it important to make things right, not just say sorry?
Can you forgive someone who hasn't said sorry?

freedom.question: What does it mean to be free? Is freedom something inside us, or something a society gives and protects?

stances.label: Freedom inside: of the mind, will or soul
Freedom in society, under law

stops.text: Herodotus tells of the Persian king Xerxes, who could not see why free Greeks with no single master would stand and fight his huge army. A Spartan exile tells him that the Greeks are free, but they have a master: their law, which they fear more than Xerxes' men fear him. For Herodotus, the Greek victory showed what free citizens can do.

Epictetus was born a slave. He teaches that the only true freedom is freedom of the will: wanting only what is in your power. A tyrant can chain the body, he says, but no one can force you to judge or choose against your will.

quote.text: And the things in our power are by nature free, not subject to restraint nor hindrance: but the things not in our power are weak, slavish, subject to restraint, in the power of others.
quote.author: Epictetus
quote.ed: George Bell and Sons, London

stops.text: Milton writes to Parliament against licensing books before they are printed. Truth is strong, he argues, and grows by meeting falsehood in open argument, so a free people should let books be published and judged. He also says that a virtue that has never been tested is not worth much.

quote.text: Let her and Falsehood grapple; who ever knew Truth put to the worse, in a free and open encounter?
quote.author: John Milton
quote.ed: printed in London; Project Gutenberg text

stops.text: Spinoza says that everything follows from causes, so freedom cannot mean acting without a cause. A person is free when they act from their own understanding instead of being pushed about by passions. The free person, for him, is the one who sees clearly.

quote.text: Human infirmity in moderating and checking the emotions I name bondage: for, when a man is a prey to his emotions, he is not his own master, but lies at the mercy of fortune…
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza
quote.ed: The Chief Works of Benedict de Spinoza, vol. II, George Bell & Sons

stops.text: Locke argues that people are by nature free and that government exists to protect their lives, liberty and property. Freedom is not doing whatever you like, he says, but living under laws you have consented to. In his letter on toleration, he adds that belief cannot be forced, so governments should not try.

quote.text: And such is the nature of the understanding, that it cannot be compelled to the belief of any thing by outward force.
quote.author: John Locke
quote.ed: A Letter Concerning Toleration, London edition

stops.text: Rousseau opens with a famous line: people are born free and are everywhere in chains. He seeks a kind of society in which each person, by joining with all, still obeys only himself. Obeying a law we have given ourselves, he argues, is real freedom.

quote.text: Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains.
quote.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
quote.work: The Social Contract, Book I, ch. 1
quote.ed: The Social Contract & Discourses, Everyman's Library, J. M. Dent, London, and E. P. Dutton, New York

stops.text: Hegel reads all of history as the story of freedom growing. In the oldest empires, he says, only one person, the ruler, was free; in Greece and Rome, some were; in the modern world, the idea is that all people are free. He thought this freedom becomes real in laws and institutions.

quote.text: The History of the world is none other than the progress of the consciousness of Freedom.
quote.author: Hegel
quote.work: Lectures on the Philosophy of History, Introduction
quote.ed: Bohn's Philosophical Library, London (1884 printing)

stops.text: Mill worries less about kings than about the pressure of public opinion. His principle: society may limit a person's freedom only to prevent harm to others, not for that person's own good. He defends free speech because even a wrong opinion can help us understand the truth better.

quote.text: That the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.
quote.author: Mill
quote.ed: John W. Parker and Son, London

stops.text: Ivan Karamazov tells a story about a Grand Inquisitor who says most people do not want freedom: they want bread, wonder and someone to obey. Dostoevsky, who was a believer, gives this argument great force on purpose. He answers it through Alyosha and the elder Zosima, whose free, active love shows a different way.

young: Being free means being able to make your own choices. Some freedoms come from outside: being allowed to speak, read and play. Your family and your country protect those freedoms with rules that keep everyone safe.

Another freedom is inside you. Even when you can't choose what happens, like a rainy day or a hard test, you can choose how you act and what you think. A Greek teacher who had been a slave said no one can take that freedom away.
talk: Are you more free with no rules at all, or with good rules? Think of a game with no rules.
Mill says people should be free to do anything that doesn't harm others. Can you think of a hard case?
Epictetus was a slave, yet said he was free inside. What did he mean?
Milton says truth wins in a fair argument. Do you agree?
What freedoms do you have now that you didn't have when you were little? What comes with them?

friendship.question: What is a true friend? Why do we need friends, and what kinds of love are there?

stops.text: In the Symposium, friends at a dinner take turns praising love. Socrates passes on what he says he learned from a wise woman, Diotima: love can rise step by step, from caring for one person to loving good character, then knowledge, and at last beauty itself. For Plato, love is a longing that can lift the soul upward.

Aristotle sorts friendships into three kinds: friends who are useful to each other, friends who enjoy each other, and friends who love each other for their goodness. Only the third kind lasts, because it rests on who the friends are. A true friend, he says, is like another self, and no one would choose to live without friends even with every other good thing.

Aquinas takes Aristotle's idea of friendship and uses it to describe love of God. Charity, he argues, is a friendship between a person and God, and it reaches out from there to love one's neighbor. Friendship becomes the model for the highest love.

quote.text: The love which is based on this communication, is charity: wherefore it is evident that charity is the friendship of man for God.
quote.author: Thomas Aquinas
quote.work: Summa Theologica, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 23, Article 1
quote.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province
quote.ed: Second and Revised Edition

stops.text: Montaigne writes about his friend Étienne de La Boétie, who died young. Ordinary friendships, he says, are built on usefulness or habit, but theirs was a joining of two souls that he could not fully explain. Asked why he loved his friend, he could only answer: because it was he, because it was I.

Shakespeare's sonnets praise a beloved friend and promise that poetry will keep his beauty alive. Sonnet 116 describes a love that does not change when times change. It is a steady mark that ships can steer by in a storm.

quote.text: Let me not to the marriage of true minds Admit impediments.
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.ed: Shake-speares Sonnets, London

stops.text: Boswell, a young Scot, became the friend of the great English writer Samuel Johnson, though Johnson liked to tease the Scots. Boswell wrote down their talks for years. His book shows a real friendship between two very different men, with arguments, jokes and loyalty.

In Emma, Mr. Knightley proves his friendship by telling Emma when she has done wrong, as when she mocks poor Miss Bates. Emma's friendship with Harriet, by contrast, is spoiled because Emma tries to manage her. Austen suggests that a true friend wants your good, not only your comfort.

quote.text: Her situation should secure your compassion.
quote.author: Austen
quote.ed: John Murray, London (first edition)

stops.text: Huck and Jim, a man escaping slavery, float down the Mississippi together. Huck was raised to see Jim as property, but on the raft he comes to know Jim as a kind, wise friend. Twain shows a friendship growing stronger than the rules of the society around them.

quote.text: We said there warn't no home like a raft, after all.
quote.author: Twain
quote.work: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, Chapter XVIII
quote.ed: Charles L. Webster and Company, New York

young: A friend is someone you like to be with and who wants good things for you. Aristotle noticed three kinds of friends: friends who help each other, friends who have fun together, and friends who care about each other because they are both good people.
The third kind lasts the longest. A true friend will play with you, but also tell you kindly when you are being unfair, and stay with you when things are hard.
talk: Which of Aristotle's three kinds of friendship do you have? Can one friendship be more than one kind?
Mr. Knightley tells Emma she was unkind. Is it friendly to tell a friend they did something wrong? How should you do it?
Montaigne couldn't explain why he loved his friend. Can you explain why you like your best friend?
Huck and Jim become friends even though the world around them said they shouldn't. Why do you think their friendship grew?
Can a family member also be a friend?

geometry.question: What can we prove about shapes and space? Is Euclid's geometry the true geometry of the world?

stops.text: Socrates draws squares in the sand and asks a boy how to make a square with twice the area. The boy first guesses wrong, then sees that the answer is the square built on the diagonal. For Plato, geometry shows that the mind can find truths it was never told.

Plato links the five regular solids to the elements of nature: the cube to earth, the pyramid to fire, and so on. These solids are the only ones with identical regular faces. Geometry, for him, is the plan behind the world.

Euclid starts with five postulates, such as that a straight line can be drawn between any two points, and proves theorem after theorem. Book I ends with the Pythagorean theorem and its converse. The fifth postulate, about parallel lines, puzzled mathematicians for two thousand years.

quote.text: In right-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the right angle is equal to the squares on the sides containing the right angle.
quote.author: Euclid
quote.ed: Cambridge University Press

stops.text: The last book of the Elements builds the five regular solids inside a sphere and proves there can be no others. Many think this was the goal of the whole work. It joins the geometry of Plato's Timaeus to strict proof.

quote.text: I say next that no other figure, besides the said five figures, can be constructed which is contained by equilateral and equiangular figures equal to one another.
quote.author: Euclid
quote.ed: Cambridge University Press

stops.text: Archimedes finds the area of a circle, the volume of a sphere and the area of a parabola's slice, using clever methods of squeezing a shape between figures he could measure. He was proudest of showing a sphere has two-thirds the volume of the cylinder around it.

Descartes shows how to describe curves with equations, so that geometry and algebra can solve each other's problems. Today's graphs on x and y axes grow from his idea. Hard geometric problems become calculations.

quote.text: Any problem in geometry can easily be reduced to such terms that a knowledge of the lengths of certain straight lines is sufficient for its construction.
quote.author: René Descartes
quote.tr: David Eugene Smith and Marcia L. Latham
quote.ed: Open Court, Chicago

stops.text: By Poincaré's time, mathematicians had found consistent geometries in which Euclid's parallel postulate fails. Poincaré argues that asking which geometry is true is like asking whether meters are truer than feet. We choose the one that is most convenient.

quote.text: One geometry cannot be more true than another; it can only be more convenient.
quote.author: Henri Poincaré
quote.work: Science and Hypothesis, Chapter III, Non-Euclidean Geometries
quote.ed: Walter Scott Publishing

stops.text: Einstein answers that, for physics, the geometry of space-time is something to be found by experiment, and near heavy masses it is not Euclid's. Gravity shows up as curved space-time. Geometry becomes part of physics.

young: Geometry is the math of shapes: lines, circles, triangles and cubes. Euclid, a Greek teacher, showed how to prove facts about shapes step by step, starting from simple rules.

Try this: draw a square, then draw a line from one corner to the opposite corner. Build a new square on that line. It has exactly twice the area of the first one! Socrates showed a boy this trick 2,400 years ago.
talk: Why is it not enough to measure a drawing to prove something in geometry?
Find shapes around your house: circles, triangles, rectangles, cubes. Which is most common?
Can you make a solid with all faces the same regular shape? How many kinds can you find?
What would a world look like where parallel lines could meet?

god.question: What have the great writers argued and believed about God? Can reason tell us anything about God?
god.intro: This page reports what each author argued, in their own terms. The authors disagree deeply, and families will have their own beliefs; the point here is to understand each view fairly.

stops.text: Plato's Timaeus tells of a good divine maker who shaped the world out of disorder, using eternal patterns as his model. Because the maker is good and free of envy, he wanted everything to be as good as possible. Plato offers it as a likely story, not a proof.

quote.text: And being free from jealousy, he desired that all things should be as like himself as they could be.
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. III, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Aristotle reasons that the eternal motion of the heavens needs a first source that is not itself moved. This unmoved mover is pure thought, thinking about itself, and it moves the world the way something loved moves the one who loves it. Aristotle's god does not create the world or watch over individuals.

quote.text: The final cause, then, produces motion as being loved, but all other things move by being moved.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. VIII, 2nd edition, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Plotinus teaches that everything flows from a first principle he calls the One, beyond all description. From it come Mind and then Soul, and the soul can turn back and rise toward its source. His thought later shaped both Christian and Islamic writers.

Augustine writes the Confessions as a long prayer to God, telling how he searched through pleasure, philosophy and Plotinus before coming to Christian faith. For him, God is the creator of all things, closer to us than we are to ourselves. He describes God as the one in whom the restless heart finds rest.

Aquinas holds that some truths about God can be shown by reason, and he offers five ways, from motion, causes, things that need not exist, degrees of goodness, and the order of nature. Other truths, like the Trinity, he says, are known only by revelation. Philosophers have debated his arguments ever since.

quote.text: The existence of God can be proved in five ways.
quote.author: Thomas Aquinas
quote.work: Summa Theologica, First Part, Question 2, Article 3
quote.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province
quote.ed: Second and Revised Edition

stops.text: Calvin begins by saying that nearly all wisdom is knowing God and knowing ourselves, and that each leads to the other. He holds that people have a sense of God built in, but that it is clouded, so they need the Bible to know God rightly. His Institutes became a founding work of Reformed Protestant churches.

quote.text: Our wisdom, in so far as it ought to be deemed true and solid Wisdom, consists almost entirely of two parts: the knowledge of God and of ourselves.
quote.author: John Calvin
quote.work: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book I, Chapter 1
quote.ed: Calvin Translation Society, Edinburgh

stops.text: Pascal, a great mathematician, doubts that proofs bring people to God. He offers instead his famous wager: if God exists, believing gains everything; if not, little is lost. He also says the heart knows things reason cannot, and he wrote as a committed Christian.

quote.text: Let us weigh the gain and the loss in wagering that God is.
quote.author: Blaise Pascal
quote.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 48, P. F. Collier & Son

stops.text: Spinoza defines God as the one infinite substance of which everything is a part, so that God and Nature are the same. His God does not act for purposes or answer prayers in the usual sense. Some readers called him an atheist, others a deeply religious thinker, and the argument continues.

Ivan Karamazov says he cannot accept a world in which innocent children suffer, whatever the final harmony. Dostoevsky, a believer, gives Ivan's protest full strength. He answers not with an argument but with the life of the elder Zosima and the gentle love of Alyosha.

quote.text: "It's not God that I don't accept, Alyosha, only I most respectfully return Him the ticket." "That's rebellion," murmured Alyosha, looking down.
quote.author: Dostoevsky
quote.work: The Brothers Karamazov, Book V, Chapter IV, "Rebellion"
quote.ed: William Heinemann, London

stops.text: The Swiss theologian Karl Barth argues that the Bible is not mainly human thoughts about God but God speaking to people. Human beings, he says, cannot reach God by their own reasoning. Preachers must speak of God, yet cannot do it by their own power, and that tension is the heart of his message.

quote.text: It is not the right human thoughts about God which form the content of the Bible, but the right divine thoughts about men.
quote.author: Karl Barth
quote.work: The Word of God and the Word of Man, The Strange New World within the Bible
quote.ed: The Pilgrim Press, Boston

young: People all over the world, for thousands of years, have asked about God. Many believe God made the world and loves people. Some believe in different ways, and some do not believe in God at all.

The great books are full of these questions. Some writers tried to reason about God, some prayed, and some wrote stories and poems. Your family can talk about what you believe, and why other people believe differently. Listening carefully is the first step to understanding.
talk: What questions do you have about God?
Aquinas thought reason could show some things about God. Pascal said the heart knows things reason doesn't. What do you think?
Why do you think people in every age have asked these questions?
How can we listen respectfully to someone who believes differently?

government.question: What is the best kind of government: rule by one, by a few, or by the many? And what is government for?

stops.text: Herodotus tells of three Persian nobles debating how to rule their empire. One praises rule by the people, one by the best few, and one by a single king, and the king's side wins. It is one of the earliest arguments in writing comparing kinds of government.

Plato argues that a city will be well ruled only when those who love wisdom rule, the famous philosopher-kings. He ranks other kinds of government from best to worst and describes how each can slide into the next. He was deeply wary of democracy, which he saw as easily swayed by flatterers.

Aristotle studies many real constitutions. He sorts governments by who rules, one, few or many, and whether they rule for the common good or for themselves. The best practical form, he thinks, is a mixed one with a strong middle class.

quote.text: Hence it is evident that the state is a creation of nature, and that man is by nature a political animal.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. X, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Hobbes says government exists to keep the peace and save people from a war of all against all. Any form can do this if its power is complete, but he thought a single monarch was most likely to be steady. For him, the alternative to strong government is chaos.

Locke answers that government is set up by the consent of the people to protect their rights. Its power is held in trust. If a government breaks that trust and tries to rule without law, he argues, the people may set up a new one.

Montesquieu sorts governments into republics, monarchies and despotisms, each with its own spirit. A republic depends on its citizens' virtue, a monarchy on honor and a despotism on fear. He admired England for dividing power among different bodies.

The authors of The Federalist argue for the new U.S. Constitution. Madison says a large republic, where many groups check each other and the people choose representatives, can guard against any one faction taking over. Hamilton argues for a strong, energetic president and independent courts.

Tocqueville studies American democracy at first hand. He praises its town meetings, local self-government and many associations. He also warns of a 'tyranny of the majority' and of people becoming so private that they leave public life to a distant government.

Mill argues that the best government is representative, with the people choosing those who make laws. It is best, he says, because it protects people's interests and also makes citizens more active and thoughtful. He also defended giving votes to women, which was unusual in his time.

young: A government is the group of people who make and carry out rules for a town or country. It can be one king or queen, a small group, or many people who vote.

Think of your class picking a game for recess. The teacher could decide, a few kids could decide, or everyone could vote. Each way has good and bad sides. The great books have argued about these choices for over two thousand years.
talk: What is government for? Make a list together.
If your family were a country, what kind of government would it be?
Plato wanted the wisest people to rule. Aristotle liked a mix. Which do you think works better, and why?
Why might a big group of people make better choices than one person? Why might it make worse ones?
What did Tocqueville admire about American towns?

happiness.question: What makes a whole life go well? Is happiness pleasure, goodness, or something else?

stops.text: Herodotus tells how the wise Athenian Solon visited the rich king Croesus. Croesus expected to be called the happiest of men, but Solon named ordinary people who had lived and died well. Wait until the end of a life, Solon warns, before you call it happy.

quote.text: before he comes to his end it is well to hold back and not to call him yet happy but only fortunate.
quote.author: Herodotus
quote.ed: Macmillan

stops.text: Aristotle says everyone wants happiness, but people disagree about what it is: pleasure, honor or money. His answer is that happiness is a whole life of activity in keeping with virtue, with friends and enough good things around it. It is not a feeling that comes and goes but the shape of a life well lived.

Epictetus, a freed slave, teaches that happiness depends only on what is in our power: our own judgments and choices. Health, money and other people's opinions are not in our power, so a wise person does not stake happiness on them. The Stoics agree with Aristotle that virtue matters most, but they say virtue alone is enough.

quote.text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.
quote.author: Epictetus
quote.ed: George Bell and Sons, London

stops.text: Augustine looks back on years of chasing success and pleasure and says none of it gave him rest. He concludes that people are made for God and that only in God can the heart be at peace. Happiness, for him, is a gift found in loving the right things in the right order.

quote.text: Thou awakest us to delight in Thy praise; for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.
quote.author: Augustine
quote.ed: A Library of Fathers of the Holy Catholic Church, John Henry Parker, Oxford

stops.text: Aquinas works through the candidates one by one: wealth, honor, fame, power, bodily goods and pleasure. Each falls short of a complete good. He accepts much of Aristotle's picture of happiness in this life but argues that perfect happiness lies only in knowing God.

quote.text: It is impossible for man's happiness to consist in wealth.
quote.author: Thomas Aquinas
quote.work: Summa Theologica, First Part of the Second Part, Question 2, Article 1
quote.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province
quote.ed: Second and Revised Edition

stops.text: Mill holds that happiness is the goal of right action, and by happiness he means pleasure and freedom from pain. He answers the critics who call this a philosophy fit for pigs: some pleasures, such as those of the mind and of kindness, are higher than others. Those who have known both kinds, he says, prefer the higher.

quote.text: It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.
quote.author: Mill
quote.ed: Parker, Son and Bourn, London

stops.text: Tolstoy's characters look for happiness in glory, in society and in big ideas. Prince Andrei, lying wounded on a battlefield, suddenly sees the sky and feels how small his ambitions were. By the end of the novel, Pierre and others find a quieter happiness in family, work and simple days.

quote.text: How was it I did not see that lofty sky before?
quote.author: Tolstoy
quote.work: War and Peace, Book Three, Chapter XVI
quote.ed: Oxford University Press (World's Classics)

stops.text: Chekhov shows people on a country estate who feel their lives have been wasted. He offers no big answer. At the end, Sonya tells her uncle that they will keep working, bear what they must, and hope for rest, and the play leaves us to judge whether that is despair or a kind of courage.

quote.text: Yes, we shall live, Uncle Vanya.
quote.author: Chekhov
quote.ed: Plays by Anton Tchekoff (Charles Scribner's Sons, New York)

young: What makes you happy? Maybe ice cream, a new game or a day at the beach. Those are good, but they don't last long. The great books ask a bigger question: what makes a whole life happy, from start to finish?

Many of the writers say it is less about getting things and more about being a good person, having good friends and doing work you care about. Think of a grandparent who has had a long, kind life with a loving family. Many people would call that a happy life, even if it had hard days in it.
talk: Solon said you can't call someone happy until their life is over. What do you think he meant?
Is being happy the same as having fun?
Epictetus says to care most about what is in your power. What things in your day are in your power, and what things aren't?
Mill says some pleasures are higher than others. Do you agree? Which ones?
Who is the happiest person you know? What makes their life go well?

heavens.question: How are the sun, moon, planets and stars arranged, and what makes them move?

stances.label: Earth at the center
Sun at the center

heavens.stance_note: Uncolored stops go beyond that question: gravity as curved space-time, and a universe of many galaxies.

stops.text: In the Timaeus, Plato tells a story of a divine craftsman shaping the world as a living whole, with the earth at the center. The heavenly bodies move in circles, which he thought the most perfect motion. Their regular paths make time and give people a model of order.

Aristotle gives evidence that the earth is a sphere: its shadow on the moon in an eclipse is always curved, and new stars appear as you travel south. He places the earth, unmoving, at the center, with the heavens made of a special element that moves forever in circles.

quote.text: How else would eclipses of the moon show segments shaped as we see them?
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: Oxford, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Ptolemy builds a full mathematical model of the heavens with the earth at the center. To match what astronomers saw, such as planets seeming to loop backward, he adds small circles riding on larger ones. His tables predicted planet positions well enough to be used for some 1,400 years.

Dante rises through the nine heavens of the medieval picture: the moon, the planets, the sun, the fixed stars and beyond. He uses the astronomy of his day as a ladder of light and joy. The poem ends with the love that moves the sun and the other stars.

quote.text: But yet the will roll'd onward, like a wheel In even motion, by the Love impell'd, That moves the sun in heav'n and all the stars.
quote.author: Dante
quote.work: Paradiso, Canto XXXIII (the last lines of the Comedy)
quote.ed: The Vision, London

stops.text: Copernicus puts the sun near the center and the earth among the planets, turning daily and circling yearly. This explains the planets' backward loops simply, as the earth overtaking or being overtaken. He still used circles and some small epicycles, and his idea took decades to win wide acceptance.

Kepler, working from Tycho Brahe's careful observations, found that planets move in ellipses with the sun at one focus, and faster when they are closer to it. His Epitome teaches the whole sun-centered system with these laws. He also guessed that a force from the sun drives the planets.

Newton shows that one law of gravity explains both an apple's fall and the moon's orbit. From it he derives Kepler's laws, the tides and the paths of comets. The heavens and the earth now follow the same physics.

Einstein's general theory describes gravity as the bending of space and time by mass. It explained a small puzzle in Mercury's orbit and predicted that starlight would bend near the sun, which was observed in 1919. Newton's law remains an excellent approximation for most purposes.

Eddington explains for general readers the new discovery that distant galaxies are moving away from us, so that the universe is expanding. The heavens are far larger than earlier astronomers imagined, and they have a history. He also wrote with wonder about what this meant for our place in it.

young: Look up on a clear night: the stars seem to turn around us, and the sun seems to travel across the sky by day. For a long time, most people thought the earth stood still in the middle of everything.

Then astronomers like Copernicus, Kepler and Galileo showed that the earth spins and travels around the sun. Try it: walk in a circle around a lamp while spinning slowly. The lamp seems to move around you, but you are the one moving!
talk: Why did it make sense for people long ago to think the sun moved around the earth?
Aristotle used a lunar eclipse to show the earth is round. How does that work?
What would it take to change your mind about something everyone believes?
Dante saw the heavens as full of meaning. How do the stars make you feel?

heroes.question: What makes someone a hero? And how did the idea of a hero change from Achilles to Huck Finn?

stops.text: Achilles is the greatest warrior at Troy, fast, strong and proud. He fights for honor and lasting fame, and he knows he will die young. Homer's hero is magnificent but flawed, and only at the end does he learn pity.

Odysseus is a different kind of hero: clever, patient and full of tricks. He survives by his wits, outsmarting the Cyclops and finding his way home. His heroism is endurance and loyalty to his family.

quote.text: Tell me, O muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy.
quote.author: Homer
quote.ed: Longmans, Green

stops.text: Virgil's Aeneas is a hero of duty. He carries his father, leads his people and gives up what he wants to found a new nation. He is less dazzling than Achilles but more responsible.

quote.text: Arms, and the man I sing, who, forc’d by fate, And haughty Juno’s unrelenting hate, Expell’d and exil’d, left the Trojan shore.
quote.author: Virgil
quote.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 13, P. F. Collier & Son

stops.text: Plutarch's heroes are real people: lawgivers, generals and statesmen of Greece and Rome. He shows their virtues and their faults, and pairs a Greek with a Roman so readers can compare. His Lives taught later readers, including Shakespeare and the American founders, about greatness.

In Henry V, the young king who once ran wild becomes a leader who inspires his tired soldiers. On the night before battle he walks among them in disguise. Shakespeare shows a hero who calls ordinary men his brothers.

Don Quixote has read so many tales of knights that he sets out to be one, and attacks windmills he thinks are giants. Cervantes makes fun of old hero stories, yet the old man's kindness and ideals win readers' love. Who is the real hero: the dreamer or his sensible squire, Sancho?

quote.text: "what we see there are not giants but windmills, and what seem to be their arms are the sails that turned by the wind make the millstone go."
quote.author: Cervantes
quote.work: Don Quixote, Part One, Chapter VIII
quote.ed: Smith, Elder, London

stops.text: Huck Finn is a poor, uneducated boy, not a knight or a king. His heroism is quiet: he protects his friend Jim against what his whole society tells him. Twain makes a hero out of plain decency.

Shaw's Joan of Arc is a farm girl who leads armies, crowns a king and is burned for heresy, then named a saint centuries later. Shaw presents her as a person of genius and common sense whom the powers of her day could not understand.

quote.text: She is the most notable Warrior Saint in the Christian calendar, and the queerest fish among the eccentric worthies of the Middle Ages.
quote.author: Shaw
quote.ed: Brentano's, New York

young: A hero is someone who does something brave or good, often for others. Some heroes are strong, like Achilles. Some are clever, like Odysseus. Some are loyal, kind or honest.
You don't need a sword to be a hero! Huck Finn was a hero because he stood by his friend. Who are the heroes in your life?
talk: Who is your favorite hero from a story? Why?
Achilles was strong but proud. Can a hero have faults?
Don Quixote thought windmills were giants. Is he a hero or a fool, or both?
What makes an everyday hero?
Would you rather be strong like Achilles or clever like Odysseus?

history.question: How do we find out what happened in the past, and why? Can history teach us anything?

stops.text: Herodotus is called the father of history. His word for his work, historiē, means inquiry. He traveled, asked questions and told what different peoples said, sometimes adding that he didn't believe a story himself. He wanted great deeds not to be forgotten.

Thucydides tried to be more exact than Herodotus. He checked eyewitness accounts against each other and left out stories he thought were fables. He wrote, he said, a possession for all time, hoping it would help future readers understand events like these.
Plutarch says he writes lives, not histories. A small saying or a joke may show character better than a great battle. History, for him, is a gallery of examples to learn from.

quote.text: It must be borne in mind that my design is not to write histories, but lives.
quote.author: Plutarch
quote.tr: John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough
quote.ed: Everyman’s Library, J. M. Dent, vol. II

stops.text: Tacitus promises to write without anger or bias, though he lived under the emperors he describes. He shows how fear bent the truth and how a few honest people held to their principles. His sharp, short sentences are famous.

quote.text: Hence my purpose is to relate a few facts about Augustus—more particularly his last acts, then the reign of Tiberius, and all which follows, without either bitterness or partiality, from any motives to which I am far removed.
quote.author: Tacitus
quote.tr: Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb
quote.ed: Macmillan and Co.

stops.text: Augustine reads all of history as the story of two cities, the earthly and the heavenly, mixed together until the end of time. History, for him, has a direction and a meaning given by God. It was one of the first full philosophies of history.

Gibbon writes the history of Rome's long fall, based on careful reading of ancient sources. He blames many causes: overgrown size, armies that made emperors, and, controversially, changes in religion. His elegant style made history a great work of literature.

quote.text: But the decline of Rome was the natural and inevitable effect of immoderate greatness.
quote.author: Edward Gibbon
quote.work: General Observations on the Fall of the Roman Empire in the West (after ch. XXXVIII)
quote.ed: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, with notes by H. H. Milman (Project Gutenberg text)

stops.text: Hegel argues that history is not random but the unfolding of freedom through the rise and fall of peoples. Yet he also says peoples and governments rarely learn anything from history. Each age faces its own situation.

quote.text: But what experience and history teach is this,—that peoples and governments never have learned anything from history, or acted on principles deduced from it.
quote.author: Hegel
quote.work: Lectures on the Philosophy of History, Introduction
quote.ed: Bohn's Philosophical Library, London (1884 printing)

stops.text: Marx and Engels read history as a series of struggles between economic classes, each era shaped by how people produce goods. Their view has influenced many historians, and many others have challenged it.

Tolstoy breaks off his novel to argue with historians. They say great men make history, he complains, but history comes from the actions of countless ordinary people. No single cause can explain a war.
Huizinga tries to recover how people of the late Middle Ages felt: their colors, sounds, ceremonies and moods. History, for him, includes the feel of an age, not just its wars and kings.

quote.text: To the world when it was half a thousand years younger, the outlines of all things seemed more clearly marked than to us.
quote.author: Johan Huizinga
quote.work: The Waning of the Middle Ages, Chapter I
quote.ed: Edward Arnold, London

young: History is the story of what happened in the past. Historians are like detectives: they look for clues, like old letters, buildings and objects, and ask people what they remember.
Not every story about the past is true, so historians check their clues carefully. Try being a historian: ask a grandparent about when they were your age, and write down what they say.
talk: Why is it important to remember the past?
Herodotus wrote down stories even when he wasn't sure they were true. Was that a good idea?
Can history teach us lessons? Hegel had doubts. What do you think?
Tolstoy thought ordinary people shape history. How do you shape your family's history?
What clues would a future historian find about your life?

human-nature.question: What is a human being? What sets us apart from other animals, and are we good or selfish at heart?

stops.text: A chorus in Antigone sings of human wonder: people sail the seas, plow the land, tame horses, invent speech and build cities. Only death defeats them. But the song warns that this cleverness can serve good or evil.

quote.text: Wonders are many, and none is more wonderful than man.
quote.author: Sophocles
quote.ed: Cambridge University Press

stops.text: Aristotle says humans are the animal with reason and speech, made to live in communities and talk about what is just. Bees and cattle live in groups too, but only humans argue about good and bad.

Machiavelli writes that, in general, people are ungrateful, changeable and eager for gain. A prince who counts on their goodness will fail. Whether he meant it as a full picture of human nature or a working rule for rulers is debated.

Montaigne studies human nature by studying himself, in all his changing moods. He finds people inconsistent, often foolish and not so different from animals. His honesty about it makes him kind toward others.

quote.text: Thus, reader, myself am the matter of my book: there's no reason thou shouldst employ thy leisure about so frivolous and vain a subject.
quote.author: Montaigne
quote.tr: Charles Cotton, revised by William Carew Hazlitt
quote.ed: Reeves and Turner, London

stops.text: Hobbes paints people as driven by desire and fear, each seeking their own good. Without a government to keep order, they would live in constant fear of one another. His view is not that people are wicked, but that they need peace and rules.
Pascal says a human being is both great and wretched: weak as a reed but able to think about the whole universe. That mix of greatness and misery is, for him, the key puzzle of human nature.

quote.text: Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed.
quote.author: Blaise Pascal
quote.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 48, P. F. Collier & Son

stops.text: In the last voyage, Gulliver meets wise, calm horses and filthy, greedy creatures that look like people. He comes home so disgusted with humankind that he prefers his horses. Swift's satire asks whether people live up to the name of reasoning animals.

Rousseau answers Hobbes. He imagines early people as simple, peaceful and kind, and blames society, property and competition for making them vain and cruel. Critics replied that his picture of natural goodness was a guess.

Darwin argues that humans share ancestors with other animals and differ from them in degree, not kind. Yet he names the moral sense as the most important human trait, one that leads people to risk their lives for others.

quote.text: It is the most noble of all the attributes of man, leading him without a moment's hesitation to risk his life for that of a fellow-creature ...
quote.author: Darwin
quote.work: The Descent of Man, Chapter IV
quote.ed: John Murray, London (first edition)

stops.text: Freud claims that people are moved by unconscious wishes far more than they realize. He calls this a blow to human pride, like the discoveries of Copernicus and Darwin. Many of his theories are now doubted, but the debate he started about hidden motives continues.

quote.text: But the third and most irritating insult is flung at the human mania of greatness by present-day psychological research, which wants to prove to the "I" that it is not even master in its own home.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud
quote.work: A General Introduction to Psychoanalysis, Lecture XVIII
quote.tr: anonymous, with a preface by G. Stanley Hall
quote.ed: Boni and Liveright, New York

young: What makes people people? We can talk, laugh, make up stories, build things and ask big questions like this one. Other animals are amazing too, but they don't write books!
The great writers argue about whether people are good at heart or selfish at heart. Some say we're born kind, some say we need rules to be good, and many say we're a mix. What do you think?
talk: What can people do that no other animal can?
Are people mostly kind or mostly selfish? Give examples.
Pascal says we are weak like a reed but can think. Why does thinking make us great?
Hobbes and Rousseau disagree about people without rules. What would happen at recess with no rules?
What do people share with animals?

journeys.question: Why do so many great stories involve a journey? What do travelers find, and what do they bring home?

stops.text: Odysseus takes ten years to sail home from Troy, facing monsters, storms and temptations. He escapes the Cyclops by calling himself 'Nobody.' The journey home is also a journey back to who he is.

quote.text: Cyclops, you ask my name and I will tell it you; give me, therefore, the present you promised me; my name is Noman; this is what my father and mother and my friends have always called me.
quote.author: Homer
quote.ed: Longmans, Green

stops.text: Aeneas journeys from fallen Troy to Italy to found a new home for his people. Unlike Odysseus, he can never go back. His journey is toward a future he will not live to see.

quote.text: Long labors, both by sea and land, he bore, And in the doubtful war, before he won The Latian realm, and built the destin’d town;
quote.author: Virgil
quote.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 13, P. F. Collier & Son

stops.text: Dante finds himself lost in a dark wood in the middle of his life. Guided by the poet Virgil, he travels down through Hell, up the mountain of Purgatory and into Heaven. The journey is a picture of a soul's path from being lost to being found.

quote.text: In the midway of this our mortal life, I found me in a gloomy wood, astray Gone from the path direct ...
quote.author: Dante
quote.ed: The Vision, London

stops.text: Thirty pilgrims ride together from London to Canterbury in spring, telling stories to pass the time. The journey is real, holy and also lots of fun. Chaucer shows how a shared road brings very different people together.

quote.text: Than longen folk to goon on pilgrimages ...
quote.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
quote.work: The Canterbury Tales, General Prologue, lines 1–2 and 12–18
quote.ed: The Complete Works, ed. W. W. Skeat, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Don Quixote and Sancho Panza ride out across Spain looking for adventures. Each inn and road brings a new misunderstanding. Their wandering becomes a long conversation between a dreamer and a realist.

Gulliver sails to lands of tiny people, giants, floating islands and talking horses. Each strange place is a mirror that shows the faults of England and of humankind. The journey makes him see home with new eyes, not all of them happy.
Ishmael goes to sea whenever he feels gloomy. He joins the whaling ship Pequod, which sails around the world on Ahab's hunt. The voyage becomes a search for meaning in a vast, mysterious ocean.

quote.text: Some years ago—never mind how long precisely—having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world.
quote.author: Melville
quote.ed: Harper and Brothers, New York (first American edition)

stops.text: Huck and Jim float down the Mississippi on a raft, Huck escaping his father and Jim escaping slavery. The river is freedom and friendship; the towns on shore are full of cons and cruelty. At the end Huck plans to head west rather than be 'sivilized.'

Marlow travels up a great African river to find a trader named Kurtz. The journey into the jungle becomes a journey into the darkness that greed and power can bring out in people. It is a story for older readers.

quote.text: Going up that river was like traveling back to the earliest beginnings of the world, when vegetation rioted on the earth and the big trees were kings.
quote.author: Conrad
quote.ed: Youth: A Narrative, and Two Other Stories (William Blackwood and Sons, Edinburgh and London)

young: Lots of great stories are about journeys: a hero leaves home, has adventures and comes back changed. Odysseus sailed for ten years to get home. Dante walked through the whole afterlife!
Journeys teach us things: about new places, about friends and about ourselves. Even a trip to a new park can be a little adventure. Draw a map of a journey you have taken, real or imagined.
talk: What is the best trip you've ever taken? What did you learn?
Why do so many stories have journeys in them?
Odysseus wanted to go home. Aeneas could never go back. Which journey would be harder?
If you could travel to one of Gulliver's lands, which would you pick?
How does traveling change the way you see home?

justice.question: What is justice? Is it built into nature, or is it something people agree on?

stances.label: Rooted in nature, reason or God
Made by agreement or by power
Partly both

justice.stance_note: Uncolored stops don't sit neatly on either side.

stops.text: Aeschylus tells how one killing in the house of Atreus leads to another, each one called justice by the person who strikes. At the end the goddess Athena sets up a court of citizens to judge Orestes. The cycle of revenge gives way to a public trial, and the Furies are given an honored place in the city instead of hunting the guilty on their own.

quote.text: Hear now my ordinance, people of Attica, as you judge the first trial for bloodshed.
quote.author: Aeschylus
quote.ed: Loeb Classical Library, Heinemann and G. P. Putnam's Sons

stops.text: In Thucydides' history, Athenian envoys tell the small island of Melos to surrender. They say talk of right only matters between equals in power; otherwise the strong take what they can. Thucydides reports the argument without cheering for it, and his readers have argued ever since about what he thought of it.

quote.text: since you know as well as we do that right, as the world goes, is only in question between equals in power, while the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
quote.author: Thucydides
quote.work: History of the Peloponnesian War, Book V
quote.ed: J. M. Dent and Sons (Everyman's Library)

stops.text: In the Republic, Thrasymachus claims justice is just a name for whatever helps the people in charge, and Glaucon asks whether anyone would stay just if a magic ring made them invisible. Socrates answers by picturing a city and a soul in good order. Justice, he argues, is each part doing its own work, with reason in charge, and it is a kind of health that makes the just person better off.

quote.text: I proclaim that justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger.
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. III, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Aristotle answers Plato with careful distinctions. Fair sharing gives each person a share that fits what they bring, and fair correcting restores the balance when someone has been wronged. He also says that some of what is just in a city holds by nature everywhere, while some is fixed by local law and could have been settled another way.

Augustine writes after Rome has been sacked. Without justice, he says, a kingdom is no better than a gang of robbers on a large scale. For him, full justice means giving God what is due to God, and he holds that every earthly city falls short of it.

quote.text: Justice being taken away, then, what are kingdoms but great robberies?
quote.author: Augustine
quote.work: The City of God, Book IV, chapter 4
quote.ed: A Select Library of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, vol. II, The Christian Literature Company, Buffalo

stops.text: Thomas Aquinas teaches that a natural law, known by reason, stands behind the laws of cities. Good human laws apply it to local needs. A command that goes against it, he argues, is not truly a law but a corruption of law.

Hobbes disagrees sharply with the older view. In a state of nature, with no government, he says nothing can be called unjust, because there are no agreements yet and no one to enforce them. Justice begins when people make covenants and set up a sovereign strong enough to make everyone keep them.

Rousseau also starts from an agreement, but a different one. A rightful order, he argues, comes from a social contract in which free and equal people bind themselves to the general will, the will of the whole people for the common good. Force alone can never make a right.

Mill admits that justice feels different from ordinary usefulness: it feels stern and binding. He argues that this feeling protects the most important parts of the general good, such as security and the rights that society should defend for each person. So for Mill justice rests on the happiness of all, not on a separate law of nature.

young: Justice is about being fair. If three friends share a pizza, it is fair for each to get the same number of slices. If one friend paid for most of it, some people think that friend should get a little more. Both ideas are about fairness, and the great books argue about which one fits when.

Justice is also about fixing a wrong. If you break your brother's toy, being fair means saying sorry and helping to fix it or replace it. Long ago, in a famous Greek play, people learned to settle wrongs in a court with a fair trial, instead of getting even on their own.
talk: Is something fair because the rules say so, or do we make rules because some things are already fair?
Glaucon asks what you would do with a ring that made you invisible. What would you do, and why?
When is it fair to give everyone the same, and when is it fair to give more to some people?
Why might a trial be better than getting even?
Can a law ever be unfair? How would you tell?

knowledge.question: What is knowledge, and where does it come from: from reason, from the senses, or from both?

stances.label: Mainly from reason
Mainly from the senses and experience
From both working together

stops.text: Plato pictures prisoners in a cave who see only shadows on a wall and take them for real things. The senses, he says, show us shadows; real knowledge is of unchanging truths, which the mind reaches by reasoning. Education is the slow climb out of the cave into the sunlight.

Aristotle begins with the senses: we love seeing even when it is useless. Experience builds up from many memories, but knowledge proper means grasping the reasons and causes behind things. Unlike Plato, he looks for the general truths inside the things we see.

quote.text: All men by nature desire to know.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. VIII, 2nd edition, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Descartes sets aside everything that could possibly be doubted, including the senses. What survives is that he is thinking, so he must exist. From there he tries to rebuild knowledge on ideas so clear and distinct that reason cannot doubt them.

quote.text: I am, I exist, is necessarily true each time it is expressed by me, or conceived in my mind.
quote.author: René Descartes
quote.ed: Descartes' Meditations and Selections from the Principles of Philosophy, Open Court

stops.text: Locke denies that we are born with any ideas built in. The mind starts like blank paper, and all its ideas come from experience: from the senses and from noticing our own thinking. Knowledge is then the mind seeing how its ideas agree or disagree.

quote.text: To this I answer, in one word, from experience: in that all our knowledge is founded, and from that it ultimately derives itself.
quote.author: John Locke
quote.ed: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Thomas Tegg, London

stops.text: Berkeley pushes Locke further. If all we ever know are our ideas, he asks, what sense does it make to speak of matter existing apart from any mind? For him, to be is to be perceived, and the steady order of the world comes from God.

Hume divides knowledge into two kinds: relations of ideas, as in math, which are certain, and matters of fact, which rest on experience. We expect the sun to rise because it always has, but reason cannot prove it will. Habit, not logic, carries us from the past to the future.

quote.text: Custom, then, is the great guide of human life.
quote.author: David Hume
quote.ed: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, reprinted from the edition of 1777, Open Court, Chicago

stops.text: Kant says Hume woke him from his slumber. He agrees that knowledge begins with experience, but argues that the mind supplies its own forms, such as space, time and cause, that shape all experience. Neither the senses nor reason can give knowledge alone.

quote.text: Thoughts without content are void; intuitions without conceptions, blind.
quote.author: Immanuel Kant
quote.work: Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Logic, Introduction
quote.ed: Critique of Pure Reason, Bohn's Philosophical Library (Project Gutenberg text)

stops.text: Russell begins by asking whether anything can be known for certain. He separates knowing things directly, by acquaintance, from knowing about them through descriptions. He holds that some general truths, such as logic, are known by reason, while most of what we know rests on the senses.

quote.text: Is there any knowledge in the world which is so certain that no reasonable man could doubt it?
quote.author: Bertrand Russell
quote.work: The Problems of Philosophy, Chapter I
quote.ed: Williams and Norgate, London (Home University Library)

young: How do you know your dog is in the yard? You can see him and hear him bark. That's knowing by your senses. How do you know 2 + 2 = 4? You can figure it out in your head. That's knowing by reason.
For a long time, thinkers argued about which way of knowing comes first. Many ended up saying we need both, like two eyes working together.
talk: Name three things you know because you saw them, and three you know because you figured them out.
What's the difference between knowing something and just believing it?
In Plato's cave, the prisoners think shadows are real. Have you ever been fooled by your eyes?
Hume says we expect the sun to rise because it always has. Is that good enough reason?
How could you find out if something you read is true?

language.question: How do words get their meaning? Can words make our thinking clearer, or cloud it?

stops.text: In the Cratylus, two friends argue: are names right by nature, so that a word fits its thing, or only by agreement? Socrates plays with both sides and some funny word origins. He ends by saying we should study things themselves, not just their names.

Aristotle says spoken words are signs of thoughts, and written words are signs of spoken ones. Words differ between peoples, but the thoughts and things they stand for are the same. He then studies how words join into statements that can be true or false.

quote.text: Expressions which are in no way composite signify substance, quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, state, action, or affection.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. I, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Augustine divides everything we learn into things and signs. Words are the most important signs, and we learn about things through them. He uses this to teach how to read hard passages of the Bible, and how a speaker should teach, delight and persuade.

quote.text: All instruction is either about things or about signs; but things are learnt by means of signs.
quote.author: Augustine
quote.work: On Christian Doctrine, Book I, chapter 2
quote.ed: A Select Library of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, vol. II, The Christian Literature Company, Buffalo

stops.text: Juliet wishes Romeo had another family name, since a name is not the person. A rose would smell as sweet by any other name. But the play shows that names, and the feuds attached to them, have great power over people's lives.

quote.text: That which we call a rose By any other name would smell as sweet.
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.work: Romeo and Juliet, Act II, scene 2 (Juliet)
quote.ed: First printed in quarto

stops.text: Hobbes says that words let us reason, but also let us talk nonsense. Reasoning goes wrong when we use words without clear definitions. Like a bird caught on sticky lime twigs, he says, the more we struggle with bad words the more stuck we get.

Locke devotes a whole book to words. Many arguments, he says, come from people using the same word for different ideas, or words for no clear idea at all. Clearing up words is part of clearing up thinking.

Lavoisier and his colleagues gave chemistry a new set of names, like oxygen and hydrogen, built to show what substances are made of. He argued that a science improves when its words match its ideas and its ideas match the facts.

quote.text: Like three impressions of the same seal, the word ought to produce the idea, and the idea to be a picture of the fact.
quote.author: Antoine Lavoisier
quote.ed: William Creech, Edinburgh

stops.text: Wittgenstein argues that the meaning of a word is mostly its use in the life of a community. Words are like tools in a toolbox, each with many jobs. Many puzzles, he thought, dissolve when we see how a word is used in everyday life.

young: Words are like labels we put on things and ideas. 'Dog' means a furry pet that barks. But words can be tricky: 'bat' could be an animal or something for baseball!
Clear words help us think and talk clearly. When two friends argue, sometimes they are using the same word to mean different things. Try asking, 'What do you mean by that?'
talk: Think of a word with two meanings. Can it cause a mix-up?
Juliet said a rose would smell as sweet with another name. Do names matter?
Lavoisier made up new words for chemistry. Why do scientists need exact words?
Have you ever argued with someone and then found you meant different things?
Make up a new word for something that doesn't have one.

law.question: Where do laws come from, and why should we obey them? Can a law be wrong?

stops.text: When King Creon forbids the burial of her brother, Antigone appeals to laws older than any king. Creon stands for the law of the city, which keeps order. Sophocles sets the two side by side and lets both suffer for their stubbornness.

quote.text: For their life is not of today or yesterday, but for all time, and no man knows when they were first put forth.
quote.author: Sophocles
quote.ed: Cambridge University Press

stops.text: In his last dialogue, Plato imagines three old men planning laws for a new city. He suggests each law should begin with a preamble that explains its reason, so citizens obey because they are persuaded, not only because they are afraid. Law, for him, should be a teacher of good character.

quote.text: Tell me, Strangers, is a God or some man supposed to be the author of your laws?
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. V, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Aristotle asks whether it is better to be ruled by the best man or by the best laws. He leans toward law, which he calls reason without passion, since any human ruler can be swayed by anger or desire. But laws are general, so wise judges are still needed for cases the law did not foresee.

Aquinas defines a law as a rule of reason for the common good, made by whoever cares for the community, and made known. He describes an order of laws: God's eternal law, the natural law that reason can grasp, and human laws that apply it. Human laws, he says, should not try to forbid every vice, only the most serious harms.

quote.text: it is nothing else than an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by him who has care of the community, and promulgated.
quote.author: Thomas Aquinas
quote.work: Summa Theologica, First Part of the Second Part, Question 90, Article 4
quote.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province
quote.ed: Second and Revised Edition

stops.text: Hobbes defines law more simply: the command of the sovereign, the power that the people have set over themselves. Where there is no common power, he says, there is no law. People obey because the sovereign keeps the peace that protects their lives.

Montesquieu compares the laws of many lands. He argues that good laws must fit the people they serve: their kind of government, their climate, trade, religion and customs. This is the spirit of the laws, and he also argues that liberty needs the power to make laws kept apart from the power to carry them out and to judge.

The Constitution of the United States is a written law above ordinary laws. It sets up the government, limits its powers and gives a way to change it by amendment. It names itself the supreme law of the land, and the people, not a king, are said to establish it.

Kant turns to a law inside each person. A rational being, he says, can give itself the moral law and follow it freely, and this self-rule is what makes people worthy of respect. He ends one book by saying two things fill him with awe: the starry sky and the moral law within.

quote.text: Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe, the oftener and the more steadily we reflect on them: the starry heavens above and the moral law within.
quote.author: Immanuel Kant
quote.ed: Kant's Critique of Practical Reason and Other Works on the Theory of Ethics, 4th edition, Longmans, Green, London

stops.text: Hegel argues that laws, property, the family and the state are freedom made real in the world, not just limits on it. The first command of right, he says, is to be a person and respect others as persons. He thinks a people's laws grow out of its history.

quote.text: Be a person and respect others as persons.
quote.author: Hegel
quote.work: Philosophy of Right, section 36 (on abstract right)
quote.ed: George Bell and Sons, London

young: Laws are rules for a whole country or town, like stopping at red lights or not taking things that aren't yours. They help people live together safely.

But where do they come from? Some writers say good laws follow rules of right and wrong that are true everywhere. Others say a law is whatever the government decides. Many say a good law should have a good reason that people can understand, just as a good family rule does.
talk: What is a rule in your home? What is the reason for it?
Plato says a law should explain itself. Do you follow rules better when you know why?
Can a law ever be wrong? What should a person do then?
Why is it helpful to have laws written down?
Which is better: a very wise ruler or very good laws?

light.question: What is light, and how do we see colors? Is light made of particles, of waves, or something stranger?

stances.label: Light as a wave
Light as particles
Something of both

stops.text: Aristotle says light is not a thing that travels but a state of a clear medium, like air or water, when it is lit by fire or the sun. Color moves the lit medium, and the medium moves the eye. Seeing needs something in between.

In the Optics printed with his Discourse, Descartes explains light as a pressure passed through a medium, like a blind man's stick feeling the ground. He works out the law of refraction for light bending into glass or water. He uses it to explain lenses and the rainbow.

Huygens argues that light is a wave spreading through a fine medium, like sound but far faster. Each point on a wave sends out its own little wave, and together they make the next wavefront. This explains reflection and refraction, and he notes that light's speed is great but finite.

quote.text: This, however, is quite another thing from being instantaneous, since there is all the difference between a finite thing and an infinite.
quote.author: Christiaan Huygens
quote.ed: Macmillan, London

stops.text: Newton splits sunlight with a prism and shows that white light is a mixture of colors, each bent by a different amount. At the end of the book he asks, as a question, whether light might be made of tiny particles. For a century his view was favored over Huygens'.

quote.text: Are not the Rays of Light very small Bodies emitted from shining Substances?
quote.author: Isaac Newton
quote.ed: 4th edition, William Innys, London

stops.text: Einstein builds relativity on the principle that light's speed in empty space is the same for every observer, however they move. This simple rule changes our ideas of space and time. Light becomes the measuring stick of the universe.

quote.text: If the observer perceives the two flashes of lightning at the same time, then they are simultaneous.
quote.author: Albert Einstein
quote.work: Relativity, Part I, Section VIII, On the Idea of Time in Physics
quote.ed: Methuen

stops.text: Planck looks back on how, in 1900, he found that energy is given off in small packets called quanta. Einstein and others then showed that light itself behaves both like waves and like particles. Planck writes about how hard it was even for him to accept the new picture.

young: Light lets us see. It travels super fast, from the sun to the earth in about eight minutes.

Newton found something amazing: white sunlight is really all the colors mixed together. A prism, or a glass of water in a sunny window, can split it into a rainbow. Try it! Scientists argued for years whether light is like tiny bullets or like waves on a pond. The answer turned out to be: a bit of both.
talk: Make a rainbow with a glass of water or a hose. Where do the colors come from?
Why does a straw look bent in water?
Huygens thought light was a wave, Newton thought particles. How could both be partly right?
Why do you think we see lightning before we hear thunder?

living-things.question: What makes something alive? How are plants and animals built, and how do they grow?

stops.text: Aristotle was the first great biologist. He sorted hundreds of animals by their parts and ways of life, and noticed that dolphins breathe air and feed their young with milk like land mammals. He urged students not to turn away from studying even humble creatures.

quote.text: Every realm of nature is marvellous.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: Oxford, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Virgil's Georgics is a poem about farming: plowing, vines, cattle and bees. He describes the bee colony with love and wonder, as a little city. It mixes real farm knowledge with old beliefs, and praises honest work on the land.

Galen says growth and nutrition are shared by plants and animals, while feeling and voluntary motion belong to animals alone. He explains living processes by faculties, powers of attraction, holding, changing and expelling. It was an early attempt at a general physiology.

Harvey watches chicks form in the egg and deer embryos develop. He argues that the parts of an animal form gradually, one after another, not all at once in miniature. His motto was that all animals come from an egg.

Kant notices that living things are unlike machines. In an organism, each part both serves and is made by the whole, as a tree's leaves feed the tree that grows them. We cannot help thinking of living things as having purposes, he says, even when we study them as nature.

In the middle of his adventure, Melville's narrator stops to catalog whales, their skeletons, their size and how whalers hunt them. Some of it is good natural history and some is out of date even for his time (he insists the whale is a fish). The whale remains a wonder beyond full understanding.

Darwin argues that all living things are related, changing slowly over many generations. Individuals vary, more are born than can survive, and those with helpful traits leave more offspring. He ends by calling the tangled web of life a grand view.

Schrödinger, a physicist, asks how living things keep their order when everything else runs down. He guesses that genes are a kind of code written in a special molecule. His little book inspired scientists who later found the structure of DNA.

Waddington describes how a single fertilized egg becomes a whole animal with many kinds of cells. Genes must be switched on and off at the right times and places. He pictured development as a ball rolling down a landscape of valleys toward different fates.

young: Living things grow, eat, breathe and make more of their kind. A rock doesn't do that, but a flower, a frog and you do!

Aristotle studied animals so carefully 2,300 years ago that he noticed dolphins breathe air like we do. Try being a naturalist: watch a bird, an ant or a plant for ten minutes and write down everything you see.
talk: What is the difference between a living thing and a machine?
Aristotle said even small creatures are marvelous. What's a small creature you think is amazing?
Watch a seed sprout in a wet paper towel. What happens first?
Why do you think Virgil compared bees to a city?

logic.question: What makes an argument good? How can we reason step by step to conclusions we can trust?

stops.text: Socrates tests people's beliefs by asking questions. He gets someone to state a view, then shows that it clashes with other things they believe. The method, called dialectic, teaches that a good argument must hang together.

quote.text: For I certainly think that I and you and every man do really believe, that to do is a greater evil than to suffer injustice: and not to be punished than to be punished.
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Aristotle was the first to study the forms of argument. A syllogism is an argument where, once some things are granted, something else must follow. 'All people are mortal; Socrates is a person; so Socrates is mortal' is valid whatever the subject.

quote.text: A syllogism is discourse in which, certain things being stated, something other than what is stated follows of necessity from their being so.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. I, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Euclid shows logic building a whole science. He starts with a few definitions and postulates and proves one proposition after another, each resting on earlier ones. For two thousand years his Elements was the model of how to prove something.

Aquinas writes in the form of disputed questions. For each question he first lists the best objections to his own answer, then gives his answer and his reasons, and then replies to each objection. It is a model of taking the other side seriously.

quote.text: The existence of God can be proved in five ways.
quote.author: Thomas Aquinas
quote.work: Summa Theologica, First Part, Question 2, Article 3
quote.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province
quote.ed: Second and Revised Edition

stops.text: Descartes gives himself four rules: accept nothing as true that you don't clearly know, divide each problem into parts, go from the simplest to the hardest, and check that nothing has been left out. He wanted to reason in every field the way mathematicians do.

Spinoza writes his Ethics like Euclid, with definitions, axioms and numbered proofs. He believed that truths about God, the mind and happiness could be shown as firmly as truths about triangles. Readers admire the rigor even when they doubt the starting points.

quote.text: By God, I mean a being absolutely infinite—that is, a substance consisting in infinite attributes, of which each expresses eternal and infinite essentiality.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza
quote.ed: The Chief Works of Benedict de Spinoza, vol. II, George Bell & Sons

stops.text: Hume says logic and math can prove relations of ideas, but no amount of logic can prove a matter of fact, such as what will happen tomorrow. For that we rely on experience. His point still guides how people think about proof and evidence.

quote.text: All these suppositions are consistent and conceivable.
quote.author: David Hume
quote.ed: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, reprinted from the edition of 1777, Open Court, Chicago

stops.text: Wittgenstein, who had once tried to build a perfect logical language, changed his mind. He came to think that words get their meaning from how they are used in many different activities, which he called language games. Many puzzles in philosophy, he argued, come from taking words out of their ordinary use.

young: Logic is the art of thinking clearly. If you know all cats have whiskers, and Tiger is a cat, then you know Tiger has whiskers. That's a logical step.
Logic also helps you spot mistakes. If someone says 'my friend got sick after eating pizza, so pizza makes people sick,' you can ask: did anything else happen? Good thinkers check each step.
talk: Make up your own 'All... Some... So...' argument. Is it valid?
Aquinas listed the best arguments against his view first. Why is that a good habit?
Descartes says to break a big problem into small parts. Try it on a chore or a puzzle.
Can an argument be logical and still have a false conclusion? How?

math-and-nature.question: Why does mathematics describe the physical world so well? Is nature written in numbers and shapes?

stops.text: Plato imagines the world built by a good maker using mathematical patterns: harmonious ratios for the soul of the world and geometric shapes for the elements. Nature is beautiful because it follows mathematical order.

quote.text: He was good, and the good can never have any jealousy of anything.
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. III, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Archimedes proves the law of the lever and the law of floating bodies as mathematical theorems from a few simple assumptions. Physics, in his hands, looks like geometry. He was among the first to do this.

quote.text: Two magnitudes, whether commensurable or incommensurable, balance at distances reciprocally proportional to the magnitudes.
quote.author: Archimedes
quote.work: On the Equilibrium of Planes, Book I, Propositions 6 and 7
quote.ed: Cambridge University Press

stops.text: Ptolemy describes the motions of the sun, moon and planets with circles on circles and tables of numbers. Whether his circles were real or only a way to calculate, the mathematics predicted the sky. Astronomy was the first science built on math.

Kepler searched for the mathematical harmony of the heavens. In The Harmonies of the World he announces his third law: the square of a planet's year is proportional to the cube of its distance from the sun. He also imagined the planets singing chords as they moved.

Galileo believed the book of nature is written in mathematics. He found that a falling body's distance grows as the square of the time and that a thrown body follows a parabola. Measuring and calculating replaced arguing about natures.

Newton's book is titled Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy. From his laws of motion and gravity he calculates the orbits of planets, the tides and the shape of the earth. Nature's whole system follows from a few equations.

quote.text: The alteration of motion is ever proportional to the motive force impress'd; and is made in the direction of the right line in which that force is impress'd.
quote.author: Isaac Newton
quote.work: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, Axioms, or Laws of Motion, Laws I–III
quote.ed: Benjamin Motte, London

stops.text: Poincaré asks how far mathematics in physics is discovered and how far it is chosen. Some principles, he argues, are useful conventions, not facts. Mathematics gives physics its language, but experiment decides what the language should say.

Einstein uses a geometry of curved space-time, worked out by mathematicians decades earlier for its own sake, to describe gravity. It was a striking case of pure mathematics turning out to fit the world.

Whitehead asks why modern science arose in Europe. He suggests it rested on a deep belief that nature is orderly and can be understood, a belief he traces in part to medieval theology. Without that faith in order, he says, scientists' labors would be hopeless.
