quote.text: Without this belief the incredible labours of scientists would be without hope.
quote.author: Alfred North Whitehead
quote.work: Science and the Modern World, Chapter I
quote.ed: The Macmillan Company, New York

young: Isn't it amazing that math describes the world? The same numbers that count your toys can tell us when the next eclipse will happen.
Galileo found that a falling ball goes 1 unit in the first second, 3 in the next, then 5, then 7: the odd numbers! Add them up: 1, 4, 9, 16. Those are square numbers. Nature seems to like patterns.
talk: Where do you see math in nature? (Think of honeycombs, flowers and shells.)
Why do you think nature follows mathematical rules?
Kepler imagined the planets making music. Can math and music be connected?
Can you think of something in nature that math can't describe?

matter.question: What is everything made of? Is matter made of tiny pieces, or of something smooth and continuous?

stops.text: Plato imagines the four elements, earth, water, air and fire, as made of tiny geometric shapes: cubes, icosahedrons, octahedrons and pyramids, all built from triangles. Elements change into each other when their triangles break and recombine. It is mathematics shaping matter.

Aristotle rejects atoms and empty space. He teaches that the four elements are made of hot, cold, wet and dry in different pairs, and can turn into one another. His view was taught for nearly two thousand years.

Lucretius, following the Greek thinkers Democritus and Epicurus, teaches that everything is made of tiny atoms too small to see, moving in empty space. Nothing comes from nothing, and nothing is ever destroyed, only broken back into atoms. He gives clever everyday evidence, like clothes drying and rings wearing thin.
Bacon tests his new method on heat. Collecting many cases, he concludes that heat is a kind of motion of the tiny particles of bodies. It was a guess well ahead of its time.

quote.text: Heat is an expansive motion restrained, and striving to exert itself in the smaller particles.
quote.author: Francis Bacon
quote.work: Novum Organum, Book II, aphorism 20 (the first vintage)
quote.tr: the version edited by Joseph Devey
quote.ed: P. F. Collier & Son, New York

stops.text: Lavoisier shows that in chemical reactions the total weight stays the same. He defines an element as any substance not yet broken down into simpler ones, and lists over thirty. Water, he showed, is not an element but hydrogen and oxygen combined.

Faraday passes electric current through solutions and finds that the amount of a substance released depends exactly on the amount of electricity. The result hints that electricity and matter both come in definite units. He was careful, though, about claiming too much about atoms.

Bohr pictures the atom as a tiny nucleus with electrons in fixed energy levels, jumping between them and giving off light of exact colors. His model explained the spectrum of hydrogen. He also wrote about how the strange behavior of atoms changes the way we describe nature.

Heisenberg, a founder of quantum mechanics, explains that at the smallest scale we can't know both exactly where a particle is and how it is moving. He compares the new physics to the old Greek debates, and suggests atoms are less like little stones and more like mathematical forms.

young: Everything around you is made of matter: your chair, the air and even you! But what is matter made of?

Long ago, a Roman poet said everything is made of tiny pieces called atoms, too small to see. Here's a clue he used: a perfume bottle opened across the room can soon be smelled everywhere, because tiny bits travel through the air. Today scientists know atoms are real, and that they are made of even smaller parts.
talk: Lucretius said rings wear thin from fingers. What does that suggest?
Lavoisier found weight stays the same in a reaction. If you burn a log, where does it go?
Plato thought elements were shapes. Why do you think he liked that idea?
How could people believe in atoms before anyone could see them?

measurement.question: How did people learn to turn size, weight and time into numbers, and why does measuring matter?

stops.text: Euclid proves exact relations between solids, such as that a cone holds one third as much as a cylinder with the same base and height. He does it without any units at all, by comparing one shape with another. Measurement begins as ratio.

quote.text: Any cone is a third part of the cylinder which has the same base with it and equal height.
quote.author: Euclid
quote.ed: Cambridge University Press

stops.text: Archimedes traps the circle between polygons of 96 sides to pin down the ratio of circumference to diameter. He proves it lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7. It was the best value for centuries, and his method of closing in on a number is still used.

quote.text: The ratio of the circumference of any circle to its diameter is less than 3 1/7 but greater than 3 10/71.
quote.author: Archimedes
quote.ed: Cambridge University Press

stops.text: Ptolemy measures the heavens. He builds tables of chords, an early form of trigonometry, and uses old and new observations to set the planets' cycles. His careful numbers let astronomers predict eclipses.

Harvey does a simple calculation: how much blood does the heart push out with each beat, and how many beats in half an hour? The total is far more than the body could make from food. So, he argues, the same blood must go around and around.

quote.text: Now in the course of half an hour, the heart will have made more than one thousand beats, in some as many as two, three, and even four thousand.
quote.author: William Harvey
quote.work: On the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals, chapter 9
quote.ed: The Sydenham Society, London

stops.text: Galileo times balls rolling down ramps by weighing water that flows from a vessel during each run. The distances, he finds, grow as the squares of the times. Measurement turns a guess about falling into a law.

Pascal has his brother-in-law carry a tube of mercury up a mountain, the Puy de Dôme. The mercury stands lower at the top, showing that the weight of the air above us pushes it up. A measurement settled an old argument about whether nature abhors a vacuum.

Huygens uses Ole Rømer's timings of Jupiter's moons to show light takes time to travel. He estimates its speed as hundreds of thousands of times faster than sound. Huygens also invented the pendulum clock, which made time far easier to measure.

quote.text: But Sound, as I have said above, only travels 180 toises in the same time of one second: hence the velocity of Light is more than six hundred thousand times greater than that of Sound.
quote.author: Christiaan Huygens
quote.ed: Macmillan, London

stops.text: Swift has fun with measurement. The Lilliputians, one-twelfth Gulliver's size, calculate that he needs food enough for 1,728 of them, which is 12 times 12 times 12. Swift mocks scientists elsewhere, but here he gets the math right.

quote.text: …the emperor stipulates to allow me a quantity of meat and drink sufficient for the support of 1728 Lilliputians.
quote.author: Jonathan Swift
quote.ed: Travels of Lemuel Gulliver into Several Remote Regions of the World, Farm and Fireside Company, Springfield, Ohio

stops.text: Lavoisier weighs everything that goes into and comes out of a reaction, using balances of great precision. The totals always match. This careful weighing founded modern chemistry.

young: Measuring means finding out how big, heavy or long something is, using numbers. You might measure your height on a door frame each birthday.

Great discoveries often came from careful measuring. Harvey counted heartbeats and figured out that blood goes around the body in a circle. Try it: count your heartbeats for one minute, then do 20 jumping jacks and count again!
talk: Why did Gulliver need food for 1,728 Lilliputians, not just 12?
How could you measure the height of a tree without climbing it?
Count your heartbeats in one minute. How many in a day?
Before clocks, how might people have measured time?

medicine.question: How does the body work, and how did healers learn to understand it and help it heal?

stops.text: The Hippocratic writers insisted that diseases have natural causes, even epilepsy, which many called sacred. They watched patients carefully, noted the effects of climate, water and diet, and wrote down what they saw. The Oath bound doctors to help the sick and do them no harm.

quote.text: It is thus with regard to the disease called Sacred: it appears to me to be nowise more divine nor more sacred than other diseases, but has a natural cause from which it originates like other affections.
quote.author: Hippocrates (Hippocratic Corpus)
quote.ed: Sydenham Society, London

stops.text: Aristotle dissected animals and described their organs carefully. He watched a chick develop in the egg day by day and saw the tiny heart beating. He thought the heart, not the brain, was the center of feeling, which later anatomists corrected.

quote.text: This point beats and moves as though endowed with life.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: Oxford, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Galen, a doctor to gladiators and emperors, did experiments on animals to learn how organs work. By tying off the tubes from the kidneys, he showed that urine is made in the kidneys, not the bladder. His writings guided medicine for over a thousand years, mistakes and all.

Montaigne, who suffered from kidney stones, was skeptical of the doctors of his day, whose remedies often did more harm than good. He preferred to let nature take its course and to watch his own body. His doubts show how uncertain medicine still was.

Harvey shows that the heart is a pump and that blood circulates around the body, out through the arteries and back through the veins. He used dissection, experiments, the valves in veins and simple arithmetic. It overturned Galen's view that blood is made and used up.

quote.text: Now this I afterwards found to be true …
quote.author: William Harvey
quote.work: On the Motion of the Heart and Blood in Animals, chapter 8
quote.ed: The Sydenham Society, London

stops.text: Harvey turns to how animals develop. Studying chicks and deer, he argues that all animals begin from an egg of some kind and that parts form one after another. He could not see the cell, but he set the questions for later embryology.

quote.text: An egg is the common origin of all animals.
quote.author: William Harvey
quote.work: On the Generation of Animals, title of Exercise 62
quote.ed: The Sydenham Society, London

stops.text: Freud, a doctor of the nerves, tried to treat illnesses of the mind by talking with patients about their memories and dreams. He started a whole field of talk therapy. Later research rejected many of his theories, but the idea that talking can help some troubles of the mind lives on in other forms.

young: Long ago, people sometimes thought sickness was caused by angry gods. Hippocrates, a Greek doctor, said no: illness has natural causes we can study, like bad water or bad food.
Later, William Harvey discovered that your heart is a pump that sends blood all around your body in a loop. Put two fingers on your wrist and feel your pulse: that's your heart pumping!
talk: Why was it important to say sickness has natural causes?
Feel your pulse. Can you find it on your neck too?
The doctors' oath says first do no harm. Why is that a good rule?
Galen made mistakes that lasted 1,000 years. How do mistakes get corrected in science?

method.question: Is there a step-by-step way to find the truth? How did thinkers and scientists learn to find things out?

stops.text: Aristotle says scientific knowledge means proving things from first principles that are true and better known. But those first principles themselves come from experience, by noticing what is general in many cases. So science runs in two directions: up from observation, then down by proof.

quote.text: All instruction given or received by way of argument proceeds from pre-existent knowledge.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. I, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Euclid's method is to state a few definitions and postulates, then prove each step from what came before. Nothing is accepted just because it looks right in the drawing. His method became the model for exact reasoning in many fields.

Bacon argues that science had been stuck for centuries. He warns against the 'idols' of the mind, habits of thought that mislead us, and calls for patient gathering of observations and experiments, then rising slowly to general laws. He compares good scientists to bees, who gather and also transform.

quote.text: The bee, a mean between both, extracts matter from the flowers of the garden and the field, but works and fashions it by its own efforts.
quote.author: Francis Bacon
quote.tr: the version edited by Joseph Devey
quote.ed: P. F. Collier & Son, New York

stops.text: Descartes gives his method in four rules: accept only what is clear, break problems into parts, go from simple to complex, and review everything. Bacon starts from the senses; Descartes trusts reason and mathematics first. Both wanted a fresh start for knowledge.

Galileo combines experiment and mathematics. He rolls balls down gentle ramps and times them, then finds the mathematical rule: the distance grows as the square of the time. His dialogue shows a new science being argued out step by step.

Newton sets out rules for reasoning in natural science: don't invent more causes than you need, and treat what experiments show widely as true until new facts say otherwise. He refused to make up a hidden cause for gravity that he could not find in the evidence.

quote.text: But hitherto I have not been able to discover the cause of those properties of gravity from phænomena, and I frame no hypotheses.
quote.author: Isaac Newton
quote.work: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, Book III, General Scholium
quote.ed: Benjamin Motte, London

stops.text: Lavoisier made chemistry a science of careful weighing. He measured everything before and after a reaction and found that the total mass stays the same. Exact measurement settled arguments that words alone had not.

Darwin spent over twenty years gathering facts from breeders, fossils, islands and barnacles before publishing. He presented his theory as one long argument, answered the strongest objections he could find, and admitted what he could not explain. His method was patient evidence from many directions.

Poincaré studies the parts of a scientific theory. Some are facts from experiment, some are useful choices or conventions, and some are guesses waiting to be tested. Hypotheses are necessary, he says, but we should know which kind each one is.

young: A method is a plan for doing something step by step. Scientists use a method to find things out: ask a question, make a guess, test it, and look carefully at what happens.
Galileo wanted to know how things fall. Instead of just arguing, he rolled balls down a ramp and timed them. You can do the same with a toy car, a book and a stopwatch!
talk: Bacon compared some thinkers to ants, some to spiders and the best to bees. What do you think he meant?
Design a test: does a heavier ball roll down a ramp faster than a light one?
Why is it important to measure carefully?
Darwin worked on his idea for twenty years. Why might he have waited so long?
What's the difference between a guess and a test?

mind.question: What is the mind? How do thinking, feeling and remembering work, and how is the mind related to the body?

stops.text: Plato pictures the soul as a chariot with a driver and two winged horses: one noble, one unruly. Reason is the driver, trying to steer both. The image explains why we often feel pulled in two directions.

quote.text: And let the figure be composite—a pair of winged horses and a charioteer.
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. I, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Aristotle says the soul is to the body as the shape is to a wax seal: not a separate thing but what makes the body alive and active. He studies the powers of living things in layers: growing, sensing, moving and thinking.

quote.text: It is therefore unnecessary to ask whether body and soul are one, as one should not ask whether the wax and the figure are one…
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: Aristotle's Psychology, Swan Sonnenschein

stops.text: In Book X of the Confessions, Augustine wanders through memory as through great halls full of images, skills and feelings. He is amazed that he can remember forgetting, and that his mind is too vast for him to grasp. Memory leads him to search for God within.

Descartes concludes that he is a thinking thing, and that the mind is a different kind of thing from the body, which takes up space. This split between mind and matter shaped centuries of debate about how the two interact.

quote.text: It is a thing that doubts, understands, [conceives], affirms, denies, wills, refuses, that imagines also, and perceives.
quote.author: René Descartes
quote.ed: Descartes' Meditations and Selections from the Principles of Philosophy, Open Court

stops.text: Spinoza answers Descartes: mind and body are not two things but one thing seen in two ways. Every event in the body has its match in the mind. Understanding our emotions, he argues, is the way to be free of their rule.

Kant argues that the mind is not a blank screen but an active organizer. It arranges what the senses give in space and time and links it by concepts like cause. Without the mind's work, there would be no experience at all.

William James helped found psychology as a science. He describes consciousness as a stream, always flowing and changing, and studies attention, habit, memory and emotion. He tied the mind closely to the brain while leaving room for free will.

quote.text: It is nothing jointed; it flows.
quote.author: William James
quote.work: The Principles of Psychology, Chapter IX (The Stream of Thought)
quote.ed: Henry Holt and Company, New York

stops.text: Freud argued that much of the mind is unconscious, and that dreams and slips of the tongue reveal hidden wishes. His ideas spread widely and changed how people talk about the mind. Later researchers have rejected many of his specific claims, while some of his broad themes, such as that much mental activity happens outside awareness, are widely accepted.

quote.text: At any rate the interpretation of dreams is the via regia to a knowledge of the unconscious in the psychic life.
quote.author: Sigmund Freud
quote.work: The Interpretation of Dreams, Chapter VII
quote.ed: Macmillan, New York (3rd edition)

stops.text: In Swann in Love, a little phrase of music becomes bound up with Swann's feelings, and hearing it again later brings that whole lost time back to him. Proust's great novel explores how memory, set off by the senses, can bring back the past more vividly than effort can. Time lost can be found again in the mind.

young: Your mind is the part of you that thinks, feels, remembers and dreams. Right now it is reading these words and maybe wondering what's for lunch!

William James said thoughts flow like a stream, one into the next. Try this: close your eyes for one minute and notice your thoughts. Where did they go? The great writers have wondered how the mind works and how it is connected to the brain and body.
talk: What is your earliest memory? Why do you think you remember it?
Plato said the soul is like a chariot with two horses. When do you feel pulled two ways?
Can a song, a smell or a taste bring back a memory for you, as a piece of music did for Swann?
Is your mind the same thing as your brain? What do you think?
Where do you think dreams come from?

motion.question: Why do things move, fall and keep moving? Does motion need a push to keep going?

stances.label: Motion needs a mover to keep going
Motion keeps going unless something changes it

stops.text: Aristotle teaches that whatever moves is moved by something. Heavy things fall toward their natural place, and he said heavier things fall faster. He also argued against empty space, noticing that in a void nothing would explain why a moving thing should ever stop.

quote.text: Further, no one could say why a thing once set in motion should stop anywhere; for why should it stop here rather than here?
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.tr: R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye
quote.ed: Oxford, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Archimedes studies bodies in balance rather than in motion. He proves the law of the lever and finds the centers of gravity of shapes. His mathematical mechanics became a model for Galileo.

quote.text: Two magnitudes, whether commensurable or incommensurable, balance at distances reciprocally proportional to the magnitudes.
quote.author: Archimedes
quote.work: On the Equilibrium of Planes, Book I, Propositions 6 and 7
quote.ed: Cambridge University Press

stops.text: Aquinas builds on Aristotle's idea that everything moved is moved by another. His first way of arguing for God reasons that the chain of movers can't go back forever, so there must be a first mover. Readers still discuss whether the argument depends on Aristotle's physics.

quote.text: It is certain, and evident to our senses, that in the world some things are in motion.
quote.author: Thomas Aquinas
quote.work: Summa Theologica, First Part, Question 2, Article 3
quote.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province
quote.ed: Second and Revised Edition

stops.text: Kepler asks what physically moves the planets. He imagines a force from the turning sun that sweeps them along, weaker farther away. He was still thinking of a mover, but now as a physical force that could be studied with mathematics.

Galileo shows by reasoning and by rolling balls down ramps that, without air resistance, heavy and light bodies fall together, speeding up evenly. A ball on a level surface with no friction would roll on and on. A thrown ball follows a curve called a parabola.

Newton states the three laws of motion. A body keeps its rest or straight motion unless a force acts; force changes motion; every action has an equal and opposite reaction. With his law of gravity, these explain motion on earth and in the heavens.

quote.text: Every body perseveres in its state of rest, or of uniform motion in a right line, unless it is compelled to change that state by forces impress'd thereon.
quote.author: Isaac Newton
quote.work: The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, Axioms, or Laws of Motion, Laws I–III
quote.ed: Benjamin Motte, London

stops.text: Faraday finds that moving a magnet near a coil of wire makes an electric current, and that a current can make a wire move near a magnet. Motion, electricity and magnetism are linked. His discoveries led to electric motors and generators.

quote.text: Being left in, the needle resumed its first position, and then the magnet being withdrawn the needle was deflected in the opposite direction.
quote.author: Michael Faraday
quote.work: Experimental Researches in Electricity, First Series, paragraph 39
quote.ed: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London, vol. 122

stops.text: Einstein asks what motion means when everything is moving relative to something else. If the speed of light is the same for every observer, then time and length must change with motion. Newton's laws still work at everyday speeds.

quote.text: Events which are simultaneous with reference to the embankment are not simultaneous with respect to the train, and vice versa (relativity of simultaneity).
quote.author: Albert Einstein
quote.work: Relativity, Part I, Section IX, The Relativity of Simultaneity
quote.ed: Methuen

young: Roll a ball across the floor. It slows down and stops. Long ago, people thought this meant things stop moving when nothing pushes them.

Galileo and Newton saw it differently: the ball stops because the floor rubs against it (friction). On smooth ice it rolls much farther. Out in space, with nothing to slow it, it would roll forever! Try rolling a toy car on carpet, on wood and on a smooth tray to see the difference.
talk: Drop a heavy book and a light ball at the same time. Which lands first? Try it!
Why do you lean forward when a car stops suddenly?
Aristotle's ideas were wrong in some ways but lasted 2,000 years. Why do you think?
Newton's third law says every push has a push back. Where do you see that when you jump?

number.question: What are numbers, and what patterns hide inside them?

stops.text: Euclid's books on number define primes and prove there are infinitely many of them: for any list of primes, there is always another. He also gives a way to find the greatest common divisor, still taught today, and a rule for making perfect numbers.

quote.text: Prime numbers are more than any assigned multitude of prime numbers.
quote.author: Euclid
quote.ed: Cambridge University Press

stops.text: In The Sand-Reckoner, Archimedes sets out to count the grains of sand it would take to fill the whole universe as the Greeks pictured it. Greek numerals stopped at a myriad (ten thousand), so he invents a system for huge numbers. His point: no number is too big to name.

Nicomachus sorts numbers into families: even and odd, prime and composite, and perfect, abundant and deficient. A perfect number like 6 or 28 equals the sum of its smaller factors. His textbook taught arithmetic in schools for a thousand years.

quote.text: Number is limited multitude or a combination of units or a flow of quantity made up of units; and the first division of number is even and odd.
quote.author: Nicomachus
quote.work: Introduction to Arithmetic, Book I, Chapter 7
quote.ed: Macmillan, University of Michigan Studies, Humanistic Series XVI

stops.text: Descartes treats lengths as numbers and uses letters for them, so geometry problems become algebra. Multiplying two lengths gives a length, not an area, once a unit length is chosen. This joined number and shape in a new way.

quote.text: Often it is not necessary thus to draw the lines on paper, but it is sufficient to designate each by a single letter.
quote.author: René Descartes
quote.tr: David Eugene Smith and Marcia L. Latham
quote.ed: Open Court, Chicago

stops.text: Pascal studies a triangle of numbers in which each number is the sum of the two above it. He uses it to count combinations and to solve problems about games of chance. It is now called Pascal's triangle, though others had found it earlier.

quote.text: The number of each cell is equal to that of the cell which precedes it in its perpendicular rank, added to that of the cell which precedes it in its parallel rank.
quote.author: Blaise Pascal
quote.ed: A Source Book in Mathematics, ed. David Eugene Smith, McGraw-Hill

stops.text: Whitehead explains that mathematics began when people saw that two apples and two days share something: the number two. Mathematics is the study of such general patterns, apart from any particular things. He shows how this abstract thinking is also very practical.

quote.text: Mathematics as a science commenced when first someone, probably a Greek, proved propositions about any things or about some things, without specification of definite particular things.
quote.author: Alfred North Whitehead
quote.work: An Introduction to Mathematics, Chapter II, Variables
quote.ed: Williams and Norgate, Home University Library

stops.text: Hardy, a great number theorist, writes about why he loved pure mathematics. He uses Euclid's proof of infinitely many primes as an example of mathematical beauty. He thought his number theory was useless, but it later became important in computer security.

young: Numbers help us count, share and measure. But they also have secret patterns. Some numbers can be split into equal rows, like 12 (3 rows of 4). Others, like 7, can't be split evenly at all: those are called prime numbers.
Euclid proved over 2,000 years ago that primes never run out. And some numbers are 'perfect': 6 is perfect because 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. Can you check whether 28 is perfect?
talk: Find all the prime numbers up to 30. Is there a pattern?
Archimedes counted grains of sand to fill the universe. What's the biggest number you can name?
Build the first five rows of Pascal's triangle. What patterns do you see?
Whitehead says two apples and two days share something. What is it?

peace-of-mind.question: How can a person stay calm and steady when life goes wrong?

stops.text: Lucretius writes his poem to free readers from fear. If we understand that the world is made of atoms moving by natural laws, he argues, we will stop fearing angry gods and death. A calm mind comes from knowing how nature works.

Epictetus says we are upset not by things but by our judgments about them. So the key is to sort what is up to us, our choices and opinions, from what is not. If someone puts him in chains, he says, they can bind his leg but not his will.

quote.text: Does any man then hinder me from going with smiles and cheerfulness and contentment?
quote.author: Epictetus
quote.ed: George Bell and Sons, London

stops.text: Marcus Aurelius ruled an empire at war, yet he wrote about finding quiet inside himself. People long for a cottage in the country, he says, but a person can retreat into their own mind at any moment. There he reminds himself of what is true and returns to work calmer.

quote.text: For nowhere, either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble, does a man retire than into his own soul.
quote.author: Marcus Aurelius
quote.ed: The Chesterfield Society, London and New York

stops.text: Augustine searched for calm in success, friendship and philosophy, but his heart stayed restless. He finds peace, he writes, only when he turns to God. For him, a quiet mind is not something we make for ourselves but something we receive.

Montaigne retired to a tower full of books to sit with his own thoughts. He found his mind running off like a wild horse, so he started writing to watch it. His calm comes from honest self-knowledge, accepting his limits and taking life as it comes.

Pascal notices that people rush into games, hunting and busy work to avoid thinking about themselves. Much of our trouble, he says, comes from not being able to sit quietly in a room. For Pascal, real peace comes only when we face the big questions, and he believed it was found in God.

quote.text: Let us endeavour, then, to think well; this is the principle of morality.
quote.author: Blaise Pascal
quote.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 48, P. F. Collier & Son

stops.text: Spinoza calls it bondage when our emotions run us. The way out, he argues, is to understand the causes of what we feel, because a feeling we understand clearly loses its grip. He admits this path is hard but says it can be found.

quote.text: But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.
quote.author: Baruch Spinoza
quote.ed: The Chief Works of Benedict de Spinoza, vol. II, George Bell & Sons

young: Everyone gets upset sometimes: when a game is lost, a tower falls down or a friend is mean. Peace of mind means being able to calm down and think clearly again.

A Greek teacher named Epictetus had a good trick. Ask: is this in my control? You can't control the rain on your picnic day, but you can choose to play a board game indoors instead. When we stop fighting what we can't change, we feel calmer.
talk: What helps you calm down when you are upset?
Make two lists: things in your control today, and things that aren't.
Marcus Aurelius says you can retreat into your own mind. What would your quiet place look like?
Pascal says people stay busy to avoid thinking. Is it hard for you to sit quietly for five minutes? Try it together.
Is being calm the same as not caring?

poetry.question: How do poems and stories work? What makes a story good, and why does poetry matter?

stops.text: Homer's poems were sung aloud long before they were written down. Bards used repeated phrases, like 'swift-footed Achilles' and 'rosy-fingered dawn,' to help them compose as they sang. The poems open by calling on the Muse, the goddess of song.

Plato, himself a gifted writer, worries about poetry. Poems copy appearances, not truth, and they stir up feelings that reason should rule. He would allow only hymns and praise of good people in his ideal city, while admitting he loves Homer.

Aristotle answers Plato. Poetry, he says, imitates life in a way that teaches: it shows what could happen, not just what did. That makes it more philosophical than history. The most important part of a story is its plot, with a beginning, middle and end.

quote.text: Hence poetry is something more philosophic and of graver import than history, since its statements are of the nature rather of universals, whereas those of history are singulars.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. XI, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Virgil's early poems are about shepherds singing contests and farmers at work. He took old Greek forms and made them Roman. His careful verse became the model of Latin poetry for centuries.

Dante wrote his great poem not in Latin but in the Italian people spoke, in linked three-line stanzas. He chose Virgil as his guide, poet to poet. His choice helped make Italian a language of great literature.
A sonnet has fourteen lines with a set rhyme pattern. Shakespeare's sonnets often turn in the last two lines, which sum up or surprise. He shows how strict form can make feelings sharper.

quote.text: O, no! it is an ever-fixed mark, That looks on tempests and is never shaken;
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.ed: Shake-speares Sonnets, London

stops.text: Milton wrote his epic in blank verse, without rhyme, which he defended as closer to the great ancient poets. Blind by then, he composed lines in his head and dictated them. His poem aims to do what Homer and Virgil did, for a Christian story.

In Pirandello's play, six characters interrupt a rehearsal, looking for an author to finish their story. They insist they are more real than the actors. The play asks what a character is and who owns a story.

quote.text: Because a character has really a life of his own, marked with his especial characteristics; for which reason he is always “somebody.”
quote.author: Pirandello
quote.work: Six Characters in Search of an Author, Act III
quote.ed: Three Plays (E. P. Dutton & Co., New York)

stops.text: Eliot's Waste Land breaks the old rules. It jumps between voices, languages and quotations from older books, like broken pieces of a culture after the First World War. Readers had to learn new ways to read poetry.

quote.text: April is the cruellest month, breeding Lilacs out of the dead land, mixing Memory and desire, stirring Dull roots with spring rain.
quote.author: T. S. Eliot
quote.work: The Waste Land, I. The Burial of the Dead, lines 1–4
quote.ed: Boni and Liveright, New York

young: Poems play with sounds: rhythm, rhyme and repeated words. Stories have characters, a problem and an ending. Aristotle said every good story has a beginning, a middle and an end.
Long ago, poems were sung out loud, and singers repeated phrases like 'rosy-fingered dawn' to help remember. Try making up a short poem with a repeated line, and say it aloud!
talk: What is your favorite poem or song? What do you like about its sound?
Aristotle says poetry shows what could happen. Why might that teach us more than facts?
Plato worried stories could be bad for us. Do you think some stories are? Why?
Write a four-line poem together. Rhyme or no rhyme?
In Pirandello's play, characters look for an author. If you were a character, what story would you want?

power.question: How do rulers gain and keep power? What makes power rightful, and how can it be kept in check?

stops.text: Thucydides says the deepest cause of the great war between Athens and Sparta was the growth of Athenian power and the fear it caused in Sparta. Again and again he shows how power, fear and honor push states to act. He hoped his history would help later readers understand such times.

Tacitus writes the history of the early Roman emperors. He shows how one-man rule bred flattery, fear and spying, and how even histories were bent by those in power. He promises to write without anger or favor.

quote.text: The histories of Tiberius, Caius, Claudius, and Nero, while they were in power, were falsified through terror, and after their death were written under the irritation of a recent hatred.
quote.author: Tacitus
quote.tr: Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb
quote.ed: Macmillan and Co.

stops.text: Machiavelli writes a guide for a new prince. He asks whether it is better to be loved or feared and answers that it is safer to be feared, if one cannot be both, though a prince must avoid being hated. Some readers see a cold handbook for tyrants, others a warning or a plain report of how politics works.

quote.text: Upon this a question arises: whether it be better to be loved than feared or feared than loved?
quote.author: Machiavelli
quote.ed: J. M. Dent, London

stops.text: In Julius Caesar, Brutus joins the plot against Caesar out of fear that Caesar will become a king. Then Mark Antony turns the crowd with one speech. Shakespeare shows the power of words, and how quickly power slips from those who think they hold it.

quote.text: Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears;
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.work: Julius Caesar, Act III, scene 2 (Mark Antony)
quote.ed: First printed in the First Folio

stops.text: Hobbes argues that without a power over everyone, life would be a war of each against all. People agree to give up their right to rule themselves to a sovereign who keeps the peace. He thought that power should be very great and undivided, since a divided power leads to civil war.

Montesquieu argues that anyone with power tends to abuse it. So liberty needs power to be divided: one body makes the laws, another carries them out and another judges. Each can then check the others.

quote.text: To prevent this abuse, it is necessary from the very nature of things that power should be a check to power.
quote.author: Montesquieu
quote.ed: The Spirit of Laws, revised edition, Colonial Press, New York

stops.text: Writing to defend the new Constitution, James Madison accepts that people are not angels. So government must be given enough power to govern, and then be made to control itself. Separate branches, each with ways to resist the others, set ambition against ambition.

quote.text: If men were angels, no government would be necessary.
quote.author: Publius (Hamilton, Madison and Jay)
quote.ed: The Federalist Papers (Project Gutenberg text)

stops.text: Orwell's animal fable shows a revolution in which the new leaders become as bad as the old ones. The pigs use fear, lies and changed slogans to keep their power. Orwell meant it as a warning about how power can corrupt any cause.

young: Power is being able to make things happen or make people do things. A team captain, a teacher and a president all have some power.

Power can help people, like a lifeguard keeping swimmers safe. But it can also be misused, like a bully on the playground. That's why many writers say power should have limits: the captain must follow the rules of the game too.
talk: Is it better for a leader to be loved or feared? Why?
Why do you think the U.S. government has three branches?
Who has power over you? Who do you have power over, like a younger sibling or a pet?
Mark Antony changed a crowd's mind with a speech. Can words be a kind of power?
What stops a leader from becoming a bully?

pride.question: Is the wish to be great a good thing or a danger? When does ambition lift a person up, and when does pride bring them down?

stops.text: The Iliad begins with wounded pride. King Agamemnon takes Achilles' prize, and Achilles, insulted, refuses to fight, so many of his friends die. Homer shows honor as a real good worth wanting, and pride as a force that can ruin the very people who prize honor most.

quote.text: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans.
quote.author: Homer
quote.ed: Longmans, Green

stops.text: Oedipus saved Thebes by solving the Sphinx's riddle, and he trusts his own cleverness completely. He rushes to find a murderer and angrily rejects warnings, only to learn the truth about himself. Sophocles ends with a warning about great fortune.

quote.text: What citizen did not gaze on his fortune with envy?
quote.author: Sophocles
quote.ed: Cambridge University Press

stops.text: Plutarch's Julius Caesar is a man of huge ambition and talent. Passing a poor village, Caesar jokes that he would rather be first there than second in Rome. Plutarch admires his gifts but shows how his drive for first place helped bring civil war and his own murder.

quote.text: To which Cæsar made answer seriously, “For my part, I had rather be the first man among these fellows, than the second man in Rome.”
quote.author: Plutarch
quote.tr: John Dryden and others, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough
quote.ed: The Harvard Classics, vol. 12, P. F. Collier & Son

stops.text: Augustine sees pride, the love of self above God, as the root of the earthly city. Rome's love of glory, he grants, produced real achievements. But he holds that humility, not glory, is the way to the heavenly city.

quote.text: Accordingly, two cities have been formed by two loves: the earthly by the love of self, even to the contempt of God; the heavenly by the love of God, even to the contempt of self.
quote.author: Augustine
quote.work: The City of God, Book XIV, chapter 28
quote.ed: A Select Library of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, vol. II, The Christian Literature Company, Buffalo

stops.text: On the first terrace of Dante's mountain of Purgatory, the proud walk bent under heavy stones, learning humility. Dante meets a famous artist of painted books who admits that his fame has already passed to another. Dante, aware of his own pride as a poet, walks bent alongside them for a while.

Macbeth is a brave soldier until witches tell him he will be king. His ambition, urged on by his wife, leads him to murder, and one crime leads to another. He admits that nothing drives him but ambition itself.

quote.text: I have no spur To prick the sides of my intent, but only Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself And falls on th' other—
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.ed: First printed in the First Folio

stops.text: Milton's Satan refuses to bow to God's Son and leads a rebellion in heaven. Cast out, he still insists he can make his own heaven by force of mind. Milton gives Satan grand speeches, so readers feel the pull of pride, and then shows where it leads.

quote.text: The mind is its own place, and in itself Can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven.
quote.author: John Milton
quote.ed: 2nd edition, S. Simmons, London; Project Gutenberg text

stops.text: Captain Ahab lost his leg to the white whale and wants revenge more than anything. He will not turn back, even when Starbuck begs him to think of their families. His proud will drives the whole crew toward disaster.

Jay Gatsby rises from a poor farm boy to a rich man with a mansion, all to win back the woman he loves. His dream is huge and hopeful, but it rests on wealth, show and a past he cannot bring back. Fitzgerald leaves readers torn between admiring Gatsby and pitying him.

young: It is good to want to do great things, like win a race, write a book or help people. That wish is called ambition. Being proud of hard work you did well is good too.

But pride can turn bad when it makes us think we are better than others or that we can never be wrong. In many great stories, a hero's bad pride makes them stop listening, and that leads to a fall. Think of someone who brags so much that they stop practicing and lose the game.
talk: What is the difference between being proud of your work and being too proud?
Macbeth and Ahab would not listen to warnings. Why is it hard to listen when we're proud?
Caesar wanted to be first. Is it bad to want to be the best?
Can you think of a story where someone learned humility?
Milton makes Satan sound impressive. Why might a writer make a bad character sound grand?

progress.question: Do things get better over time? Why do great powers rise and fall?

stops.text: Lucretius tells how early people learned to use fire, build houses, speak, farm and make laws. Step by step, by trial and error, civilization grew. But he also notes that new comforts brought new wants and new wars.
Augustine wrote after Rome was sacked. He argues that no earthly empire lasts forever and that history's true goal is beyond it, in the city of God. Progress, for him, is not in empires but in souls.

Bacon imagines an island ruled by wise scientists who do experiments to benefit everyone. Knowledge, he hopes, will bring better medicine, inventions and lives. It is an early dream of progress through science.

quote.text: The end of our foundation is the knowledge of causes, and secret motions of things; and the enlarging of the bounds of human empire, to the effecting of all things possible.
quote.author: Francis Bacon
quote.ed: first published 1627

stops.text: Voltaire mocks the idea that all is already for the best. Yet he believed people could improve things by reason, work and tolerance. His famous ending, cultivate your garden, is a call to steady, practical effort.

Gibbon wonders not why Rome fell but how it lasted so long. Great size, he says, made its fall natural. He ends hopefully, though: he did not think Europe would fall back into darkness, because useful knowledge, once gained, is hard to lose.

quote.text: The story of its ruin is simple and obvious; and instead of inquiring why the Roman empire was destroyed, we should rather be surprised that it had subsisted so long.
quote.author: Edward Gibbon
quote.work: General Observations on the Fall of the Roman Empire in the West (after ch. XXXVIII)
quote.ed: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, with notes by H. H. Milman (Project Gutenberg text)

stops.text: Hegel sees history as progress in freedom, from one free person in ancient empires, to some in Greece and Rome, to the idea that all are free. Progress comes through conflict, not smoothly. Great passions drive it forward.

quote.text: ... we may affirm absolutely that nothing great in the World has been accomplished without passion.
quote.author: Hegel
quote.work: Lectures on the Philosophy of History, Introduction
quote.ed: Bohn's Philosophical Library, London (1884 printing)

stops.text: Frazer proposed that human thought moved from magic to religion to science. Many later scholars found his scheme too simple and too sure of its own age. He also admitted that the future might bring something new.

Willa Cather shows the passing of the pioneer era on the prairie. The generous old railroad builders give way to sharp young men who care only about profit. Progress brings new wealth but loses something fine.

quote.text: Any one but Captain Forrester would have drained the bottom land and made it into highly productive fields.
quote.author: Cather
quote.work: A Lost Lady, Part I, chapter I
quote.ed: Alfred A. Knopf, New York

stops.text: Whitehead says the nineteenth century's greatest invention was the method of invention itself: organized science and engineering. Progress became something planned. He also warns that a narrow view of science can miss the values that give life meaning.

quote.text: The greatest invention of the nineteenth century was the invention of the method of invention.
quote.author: Alfred North Whitehead
quote.work: Science and the Modern World, Chapter VI
quote.ed: The Macmillan Company, New York

young: Progress means getting better over time. People invented the wheel, then bikes, then cars and planes. Medicine has helped people live longer.

But not everything always gets better. Great empires like Rome grew and then fell apart. The great books ask: does the world keep improving, or does it go up and down? What is one thing that's better now than when your grandparents were young? Is anything worse?
talk: What invention do you think made the biggest difference?
Is the world getting better? How would you decide?
Gibbon asked why Rome lasted so long, not why it fell. Why might that be a smarter question?
Can a new thing make life better and worse at the same time?
What would you like to improve in the world?

reading.question: How should we read, and why do books matter?

stops.text: Plato has Socrates worry about writing. A written page can't answer your questions, he says; it just says the same thing over and over. Real learning happens in living conversation. Ironically, we know this only because Plato wrote it down.

quote.text: I cannot help feeling, Phaedrus, that writing is unfortunately like painting; for the creations of the painter have the attitude of life, and yet if you ask them a question they preserve a solemn silence.
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. I, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Augustine was amazed to see Bishop Ambrose reading silently, his eyes moving and his lips still, since most people read aloud. Later, a child's voice singing 'take up and read' leads him to open a book that changes his life. Reading, for him, can be a turning point.

quote.text: I heard from a neighbouring house a voice, as of boy or girl, I know not, chanting, and oft repeating, “Take up and read;
quote.author: Augustine
quote.ed: A Library of Fathers of the Holy Catholic Church, John Henry Parker, Oxford

stops.text: Montaigne reads for pleasure and for wisdom, and skips books that bore him. He borrows from the ancient writers freely but makes the ideas his own. His essays are a record of a reader thinking back at his books.

Don Quixote reads so many tales of knights that he loses his grip on reality. Cervantes makes fun of bad books and of reading without judgment. Yet his book is also a love letter to stories and their power.

Bacon says some books are to be tasted, others swallowed and a few chewed and digested. We should read neither to argue nor to accept everything, but to weigh and consider. His essay is quoted on our opening rung on how to read.

quote.text: Read not to contradict and confute; nor to believe and take for granted; nor to find talk and discourse; but to weigh and consider.
quote.author: Francis Bacon
quote.ed: 1625 text, as printed in The Harvard Classics, vol. 3, P. F. Collier & Son

stops.text: Milton calls a good book the precious lifeblood of a master spirit. To destroy one, he says, is almost like killing a person. Readers, not censors, should judge books.

quote.text: Who kills a man kills a reasonable creature, God's image; but he who destroys a good book, kills reason itself, kills the image of God, as it were in the eye.
quote.author: John Milton
quote.ed: printed in London; Project Gutenberg text

stops.work: How to Read a Book (1940) and the Syntopicon (1952)
stops.text: Mortimer Adler wrote a popular guide to reading actively: asking what a book says, whether it is true and what it means for you. He then helped build the Syntopicon, an index that lets readers compare what many great books say on one idea. These Great Ideas pages, in our own words, grew from his idea of reading books in conversation with each other.

young: Books let us meet people who lived long ago and far away, and hear what they thought. Reading is a bit like time travel!
Good readers ask questions as they read: What is happening? Why did that character do that? Do I agree? Try reading a story with a grown-up and stopping to ask questions along the way.
talk: What is your favorite book? Why?
Plato said books can't answer back. How can we 'talk' with a book?
Bacon says some books should be tasted and some chewed. Which book would you chew slowly?
Don Quixote believed everything in his books. Why is it important to read with judgment?
What book would you save if you could only keep one?

pages.title: Harvard Classics Daily: fifteen minutes a day

rights.question: Do people have rights just by being human? Where do rights come from, and what does government owe them?

stops.text: Aquinas does not use the modern language of rights, but he teaches that a natural law, known by reason, binds rulers as well as subjects. Human laws that break it lose their force. Later writers built on this idea of a law above rulers when they spoke of natural rights.

Hobbes says each person has by nature a right to preserve their own life, by any means. That right can't be fully given away. To get peace, people give up their right to all things and accept a sovereign, keeping only the right to defend their own lives.

Locke argues that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property before any government exists. Property begins when a person mixes their labor with something from nature. Government is formed by consent to protect these rights and loses its claim when it attacks them.

quote.text: Though the earth and all inferior creatures be common to all men, yet every man has a "property" in his own "person." This nobody has any right to but himself.
quote.author: John Locke
quote.ed: Two Treatises on Civil Government, Morley's Universal Library, 2nd edition, George Routledge and Sons, London

stops.text: Rousseau argues that force can never make a right: to give in to force is a necessity, not a duty. Real rights come from the social contract, in which each person joins with all and gains the rights of a citizen. Freedom, he says, can't be given away.

stops.when: the Declaration, 1776; the Bill of Rights, 1791
stops.text: The Declaration of Independence names rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and says governments exist to secure them by the consent of the governed. Fifteen years later the Bill of Rights listed freedoms the new government could not take away, such as speech, religion and a fair trial.

Hegel agrees that persons have rights, starting with property, but he thinks rights only become real inside a family, a society and a state with laws. Rights are not just shields against others; they are part of living freely together.

Mill defends freedom of thought, speech and choice of how to live. Interestingly, he does not rest his case on natural rights. He argues instead that these freedoms make a society happier and wiser over time.

quote.text: His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant.
quote.author: Mill
quote.ed: John W. Parker and Son, London

young: A right is something every person should be allowed to have or do, like being safe, speaking your mind or practicing your religion. In the United States, the Bill of Rights lists many of them.
Rights come with responsibilities. You have a right to speak, and others do too, so you take turns and listen. Your right to play ends where it would hurt someone else.
talk: What rights do you think every child should have?
Locke says you own your own work. If you build a sandcastle, is it yours?
Where do rights come from: from nature, from God, from the government or from agreement? What do the writers say?
What responsibilities go with the right to speak freely?

society.question: How do societies hold together? Where do classes, customs and institutions come from?

stops.text: Aristotle says people are by nature political animals, made to live together and to talk about what is just. A person who could live wholly alone would be either a beast or a god. Society, for him, is not an invention but part of human nature.

quote.text: But he who is unable to live in society, or who has no need because he is sufficient for himself, must be either a beast or a god: he is no part of a state.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. X, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Chaucer gathers pilgrims from almost every rank of English life: a knight, a miller, a nun, a cook, a lawyer, a plowman. Each tells a tale in their own style. The result is a lively, funny portrait of a whole society, its virtues and its faults.

quote.text: He was a verray parfit gentil knight.
quote.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
quote.work: The Canterbury Tales, General Prologue, lines 43–46 and 72
quote.ed: The Complete Works, ed. W. W. Skeat, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Rousseau tells a story of how people left a simple state of nature and built societies with property, rank and envy. He argues that much inequality is made by society, not nature. His critics replied that his picture of early people was guesswork.

Tocqueville is amazed by how Americans form associations for everything: churches, schools, charities, clubs and town projects. Where in France people would wait for the government, Americans join together. He thinks these groups keep a free society healthy.

quote.text: Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions, constantly form associations.
quote.author: Tocqueville
quote.work: Democracy in America, Volume 2, Part II, Chapter V
quote.ed: Colonial Press, New York (revised edition)

stops.text: Marx and Engels argue that the way a society produces goods shapes everything else: its classes, laws and ideas. They see history as a series of class struggles. This way of looking at society has been very influential and also strongly disputed.

Dickens mocks the Circumlocution Office, a government department whose skill is never getting anything done. He shows a debtors' prison where families live for years, and the rich and poor bound together in one society. His satire helped readers see institutions that needed fixing.

quote.text: Whatever was required to be done, the Circumlocution Office was beforehand with all the public departments in the art of perceiving—HOW NOT TO DO IT.
quote.author: Dickens
quote.ed: Bradbury and Evans, London

stops.text: George Eliot studies a whole English town, where the lives of a doctor, a banker, a clergyman's family and a young idealist are woven together. No one acts alone; each choice touches others. She ends by honoring the many quiet people whose good deeds are never recorded.

Frazer gathers customs and myths from around the world to trace how human thought developed. He proposed that thinking moved from magic to religion to science, a scheme that later anthropologists criticized as too simple. His huge collection still shapes how people read old customs.

quote.text: The movement of the higher thought, so far as we can trace it, has on the whole been from magic through religion to science.
quote.author: James George Frazer
quote.work: The Golden Bough (abridged edition), Chapter LXIX
quote.ed: The Macmillan Company, New York

stops.text: Max Weber studies how authority works: through tradition, through a leader's personal gifts, or through rules and offices. He thought modern life was being organized more and more by bureaucracy. He saw its efficiency and also feared that people could become trapped in a cage of rules.

young: A society is a big group of people living together, like a town or a country. People in a society have different jobs: farmers, teachers, doctors, builders. They depend on each other.

Societies also have customs, like how people greet each other or celebrate holidays. The great books ask how all these people and customs fit together, and how a society can be fair to everyone in it.
talk: Name ten jobs people do in your town. How do they depend on each other?
Tocqueville saw Americans forming groups to fix problems. What groups do you or your family belong to?
Chaucer's pilgrims came from every walk of life. What could they learn from each other on the road?
Dickens made fun of an office that never got anything done. Why can it be hard for big organizations to act?

soul.question: What is a soul? Is it something separate from the body, and does anything of us last after death?
soul.intro: The authors disagree, and many families hold beliefs of their own. Each stop gives the author's own view.

stances.label: The soul lives on after death
The soul ends with the body

soul.stance_note: Uncolored stops take a different or more cautious line.

stops.text: On his last day, Socrates gives his friends arguments that the soul is immortal: it is like the unchanging truths it knows, and it gives life to the body as fire gives heat. His friends raise objections, and he answers them calmly. Then he drinks the poison without fear.

quote.text: Are not all things which have opposites generated out of their opposites?
quote.author: Plato
quote.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Aristotle defines the soul as the life of a natural body: what an eye's seeing is to the eye. Plants, animals and people all have souls, with different powers. Whether any part of the soul, such as the intellect, can exist apart from the body, he leaves unclear, and readers still argue about it.

quote.text: For if the eye were an animal, vision would be its soul, i.e. vision is the notional essence of the eye.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: Aristotle's Psychology, Swan Sonnenschein

stops.text: Lucretius argues that the soul is made of very fine atoms spread through the body. It grows and weakens with the body, and scatters at death. That, he says, is why death is nothing to fear.

Plotinus teaches that the soul comes from a higher world and is not truly at home in the body. By turning inward, it can rise toward Mind and the One. His student wrote that he seemed ashamed to be in a body.

quote.text: Is it not enough to carry about this image in which nature has enclosed us?
quote.author: Porphyry
quote.work: Life of Plotinus, chapter 1 (Plotinus, refusing to sit for a portrait)
quote.ed: Philip Lee Warner, publisher to the Medici Society, London

stops.text: Aquinas combines Aristotle with Christian teaching. The soul is the form of the body, so a human being is one creature, not a soul trapped inside. Yet because the soul can think, which no bodily organ does by itself, he argues it survives death.

Descartes argues that the mind is a thinking thing quite distinct from the body, which is extended in space. He hoped this would support belief in the soul's immortality. How two such different things work together became one of philosophy's hardest puzzles.

William James writes as a scientist. He says psychology can study thoughts and feelings and their ties to the brain without needing the idea of a soul to explain them. He adds that this leaves the question of a soul open for philosophy and religion.

young: Many people believe each person has a soul: the deepest part of you that thinks, loves and chooses. Some believe the soul lives on after the body dies. Others believe differently.

The great thinkers argued about the soul for thousands of years. Plato said it lives forever. Aristotle said it is what makes a body alive, like the seeing in an eye. Your family can share what you believe.
talk: What do you think makes you you?
Aristotle said the soul of an eye would be seeing. What would the soul of a hand be?
Why do you think Socrates was calm on his last day?
Do animals and plants have souls, as Aristotle thought? What would that mean?

time.question: What is time? Did the world have a beginning, and why does time feel so different at different moments?

stops.text: Plato calls time a moving image of eternity. The maker set the sun, moon and planets moving so that their regular cycles would measure days, months and years. Time and the heavens began together.
Aristotle defines time as the number of motion with respect to before and after. Without change, we would not notice time passing. He held that time and motion have no beginning and no end.

Augustine famously says he knows what time is until someone asks him. The past is no longer and the future not yet, so where is time? He concludes that time lives in the mind as memory, attention and expectation, and that God created time along with the world.

Aquinas asks whether the world always existed. He argues that reason alone cannot prove either answer, so the question can't be settled by philosophy. He believed, by faith, that the world had a beginning.
Shakespeare's sonnets battle devouring Time, which wrinkles faces and topples monuments. Their answer is love and poetry, which can outlast it. The lines still live, as he promised.

quote.text: Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May, And summer's lease hath all too short a date: ...
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.ed: Shake-speares Sonnets, London

stops.text: Kant argues that time is not a thing out in the world but a form of our own experience. We can't experience anything except in time. He also shows that reason gets tangled when it asks whether the world had a beginning in time.
Bergson separates clock time, cut into equal pieces, from lived time, which flows and builds up like a melody. Science measures the first, he says, but we know the second from inside, by intuition.

quote.text: The first implies that we move round the object; the second that we enter into it.
quote.author: Henri Bergson
quote.ed: G. P. Putnam's Sons, New York and London

stops.text: Proust writes about time lost and found. In Swann in Love, a phrase of music is tied to a season of feeling that Swann later meets again. Memory, for Proust, can bring the past back whole.

quote.text: For a long time I used to go to bed early.
quote.author: Proust
quote.ed: Swann's Way (Henry Holt and Company, New York)

stops.text: Einstein shows that time is not the same for everyone. Two events that are simultaneous for one observer may not be for another moving past. Clocks that move run slow, which has since been measured with precise clocks on airplanes and satellites.

quote.text: Every reference-body (co-ordinate system) has its own particular time; unless we are told the reference-body to which the statement of time refers, there is no meaning in a statement of the time of an event.
quote.author: Albert Einstein
quote.work: Relativity, Part I, Section IX, The Relativity of Simultaneity
quote.ed: Methuen

stops.text: In the middle part of To the Lighthouse, called Time Passes, ten years go by in a few pages while an empty house slowly decays. The rest of the novel stretches single days across many pages. Woolf shows how differently time feels from outside and inside.

young: Time is what clocks measure: seconds, minutes, days. But time feels different at different moments. Waiting for your birthday feels so slow, and a fun afternoon zips by!
Augustine said he knew what time was until someone asked him to explain it. Try it yourself: can you say what time is without using the word 'time'?
talk: When does time feel slow for you? When does it feel fast?
Augustine says the past lives in memory and the future in expectation. What do you think?
If you could visit any time in the past, when would you go?
Einstein said moving clocks run slow. Does that surprise you?
Shakespeare hoped his poems would beat time. What do you hope will last?

tragedy.question: Why do people watch stories of great people brought low? What can tragedy teach?

stops.text: Aeschylus shows a family caught in a chain of crimes and revenge. The chorus sings that Zeus has made it a law that we learn through suffering. Tragedy, for him, is how wisdom is won.

quote.text: Zeus, who sets mortals on the path to understanding, Zeus, who has established as a fixed law that wisdom comes by suffering.
quote.author: Aeschylus
quote.ed: Loeb Classical Library, Heinemann and G. P. Putnam's Sons

stops.text: Oedipus, a good and clever king, sets out to find who brought a plague on his city, and discovers it was himself, without knowing it. Sophocles shows how a person can be great and still be ruined. The ending warns against calling anyone happy too soon.

quote.text: Therefore, while our eyes wait to see the final destined day, we must call no mortal happy until he has crossed life’s border free from pain.
quote.author: Sophocles
quote.ed: Cambridge University Press

stops.text: Euripides puts ordinary feelings and suffering, especially of women and the defeated, at the center of tragedy. His characters argue fiercely and are torn by passion. Aristotle later called him the most tragic of the poets.

Aristotle studies how tragedy works. The best tragedy shows a good but imperfect person falling through some error, with a reversal and a moment of recognition. It stirs pity and fear and leaves the audience cleansed, a word whose meaning critics still debate.

quote.text: Now a whole is that which has beginning, middle, and end.
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. XI, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Chaucer tells of Troilus, a Trojan prince, who loves Criseyde and loses her when she is sent to the Greek camp. He calls his poem a tragedy, a fall from happiness to misery. At the end, Troilus looks down from the heavens and laughs at how small earthly troubles seem.

Othello, a noble general, is tricked by his trusted officer Iago into believing his loving wife is unfaithful. Jealousy destroys him. Shakespeare makes the audience watch, knowing the truth, as a good man is ruined by a lie.

quote.text: It is the green-ey'd monster which doth mock The meat it feeds on.
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.ed: First printed in the First Folio

stops.text: King Lear gives away his kingdom to the daughters who flatter him and loses everything. Out in a storm, he learns humility and compassion for the poor. Many think it the greatest and darkest of tragedies.

Racine's Phaedra is torn by a love she knows is wrong and cannot master. Written in elegant verse that follows strict rules, the play shows a person destroyed by a passion she fights against. Racine based it on a play by Euripides.

quote.text: Strength fails me, and I needs must rest awhile.
quote.author: Jean Racine
quote.ed: The Dramatic Works of Jean Racine, George Bell & Sons (Bohn's Library)

stops.text: O'Neill sets Aeschylus' story of a cursed family in New England after the Civil War. Instead of gods and Furies, the family is driven by hidden feelings and the past. It shows how the old tragic shapes still speak to modern audiences.

young: A tragedy is a sad story where something goes badly wrong, often for a good person. Why would anyone want to watch that? Because tragedies help us feel for others and learn from their mistakes.
In many tragedies the hero has one big flaw, like pride, jealousy or not listening. Think of a story you know that has a sad ending. What could the character have done differently?
talk: Why do people like sad stories?
Aeschylus says we learn through suffering. Have you ever learned from something hard?
Othello believed a lie. How can we avoid being fooled?
Is a tragedy's hero to blame for what happens, or is it bad luck?

truth.question: What does it mean for something to be true? And how do we find the truth when people disagree?

stops.text: For Plato, the truest things are the unchanging Forms, and the highest of them, the Good, is like the sun that lets us see everything else. Finding truth means turning the whole soul toward it. Opinions about changing things are only half true.

Aristotle gives a plain account: to say of what is that it is, and of what is not that it is not, is true. He also defends the rule that a thing cannot both be and not be in the same respect at the same time. Without that rule, he says, no one could argue about anything.

quote.text: It is, that the same attribute cannot at the same time belong and not belong to the same subject and in the same respect…
quote.author: Aristotle
quote.ed: The Works of Aristotle, vol. VIII, 2nd edition, Clarendon Press

stops.text: Augustine tells Christian readers not to fear the learning of pagan writers. Whatever is true, he says, comes from God, wherever it is found. He compares useful learning to treasure carried out of Egypt.

quote.text: Let every good and true Christian understand that wherever truth may be found, it belongs to his Master.
quote.author: Augustine
quote.work: On Christian Doctrine, Book II, chapter 18
quote.ed: A Select Library of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, vol. II, The Christian Literature Company, Buffalo

stops.text: Milton argues that truth is strong enough to win in open argument. Licensing books before printing, he says, treats readers like children and keeps truth from growing. Truth needs to meet falsehood face to face.

Mill adds that even when we are right, we need to hear the other side. A truth that is never challenged becomes a dead slogan instead of a living belief. And the silenced opinion might hold part of the truth we lack.

In The Wild Duck, a young man is determined to reveal a family's hidden past, sure that truth will set them free. Instead it brings disaster. A cynical doctor says ordinary people need their comforting illusions, and Ibsen leaves the audience to weigh both sides.

quote.text: Rob the average man of his life-illusion, and you rob him of his happiness at the same time.
quote.author: Ibsen
quote.ed: Ibsen's Prose Dramas, ed. William Archer (Walter Scott, London)

stops.text: Nietzsche asks why we want truth at all, and whether philosophers' systems are really personal confessions. He suspects that much of what passes for truth serves the needs of those who hold it. Readers still argue over whether he meant to reject truth or to demand a harder honesty about it.

quote.text: It has gradually become clear to me what every great philosophy up till now has consisted of—namely, the confession of its originator, and a species of involuntary and unconscious auto-biography.
quote.author: Nietzsche
quote.ed: T. N. Foulis, Edinburgh and London

stops.text: William James suggests a practical test: what difference would it make if an idea were true? True ideas, he says, are the ones we can check and that guide us well through experience. His critics answered that something can be useful and still be false.

quote.text: True ideas are those that we can assimilate, validate, corroborate and verify.
quote.author: William James
quote.ed: Longmans, Green, and Co., New York

stops.text: Russell answers James. A belief is true, he argues, when it matches the facts, and false when it doesn't, whatever it does for us. Truth depends on the world, not on what we would like.

young: Something is true when it matches how things really are. If you say 'it's raining' and it is raining, that's true. If it's sunny, it isn't.

Finding the truth can be hard when people disagree. One good way is to listen to both sides, look at the evidence and be willing to change your mind. Milton thought truth wins if it gets a fair fight.
talk: How can you tell if something you hear is true?
Mill says we should listen to people we disagree with. Why might that help us?
Is it ever kind not to tell the truth? What does The Wild Duck suggest?
James asks what difference a truth makes. Can something be true but make no difference?
What is a time you changed your mind because of new facts?

war.question: Why do nations go to war? What does war do to people, and can war ever be just?

stops.text: The Iliad is a war poem, full of courage and glory. Yet Homer never forgets the cost: the widows, the orphans, the old fathers. Its last scene is a truce, as Achilles gives back Hector's body to his grieving father.

Thucydides wanted to explain the war, not just tell it. He separates the complaints people gave from what he saw as the true cause: fear of a rising power. He shows how war is a harsh teacher that changes the way people think and even what words mean.

Euripides staged The Trojan Women while Athens was at war. It shows no battles at all, only the women of Troy after the city has fallen, waiting to be taken away. The play makes the audience feel war from the side of those who lose everything.

Augustine believes peace is what every war aims at, even the wars of the wicked. A good person may sometimes have to fight a just war, he argues, but should grieve that it was needed. His thoughts became a starting point for later ideas about just war.

In Henry V, the king rallies his tired army with stirring speeches. But the night before the battle, in disguise, he hears common soldiers ask who will answer for those who die in an unjust war. Shakespeare shows both the glory and the weight of war.

quote.text: Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more, Or close the wall up with our English dead.
quote.author: William Shakespeare
quote.work: Henry V, Act III, scene 1 (King Henry)
quote.ed: First printed in the First Folio

stops.text: Hobbes describes life without government as a war of each against all, where life is nasty, brutish and short. Competition, fear and pride drive people to fight. Peace, he argues, comes only when all agree to obey a common power.

Gibbon follows centuries of wars as Rome's empire breaks apart. He shows how armies made and unmade emperors and how invasions wore down the frontiers. In his telling, war wins glory for a few and brings ruin to many.

Tolstoy sets his novel during Napoleon's invasion of Russia. He argues that great generals do not really control battles: the outcome comes from the choices of countless ordinary people. The novel moves between the chaos of the battlefield and the families waiting at home.

quote.text: History, that is, the unconscious, general, hive life of mankind, uses every moment of the life of kings as a tool for its own purposes.
quote.author: Tolstoy
quote.work: War and Peace, Book Nine, Chapter I
quote.ed: Oxford University Press (World's Classics)

young: A war is a big fight between countries or groups, with armies. Wars have caused great sadness, but stories about war also tell of courage, friendship and sacrifice.

The great writers ask why wars start: fear, pride, wanting land or wanting to protect people. They also ask how peace can be kept. On a playground, fights often start from fear or pride too, and peace comes when people talk, share and follow fair rules.
talk: Thucydides said fear caused the war. How can fear make people fight?
Why do you think The Trojan Women shows no battles?
Augustine says even wars aim at peace. What do you think he meant?
Tolstoy thought ordinary people mattered more than generals. Do you agree?
What helps people make peace after a fight?

wealth.question: What is wealth, and how is it made and shared? Is the love of money good, bad or neither?

stops.text: Aristotle separates managing a household, which gathers what a family needs, from money-making for its own sake, which has no natural limit. Money was invented to make trade easier. He criticized lending money at interest, since money then breeds money.

Aquinas argues that wealth can't be what happiness is, because it is only a means to other things. Riches are for use: to support life and to help others. Like Aristotle, he warns against a desire for money that knows no limit.

quote.text: It is impossible for man's happiness to consist in wealth.
quote.author: Thomas Aquinas
quote.work: Summa Theologica, First Part of the Second Part, Question 2, Article 1
quote.tr: the Fathers of the English Dominican Province
quote.ed: Second and Revised Edition

stops.text: Locke argues that property comes from work. When a person picks apples or plows a field, they mix their labor with nature and make it theirs. He thought labor gives things most of their value, and that money let people keep wealth without it spoiling.
