quote.text: The "labour" of his body and the "work" of his hands, we may say, are properly his.
quote.author: John Locke
quote.ed: Two Treatises on Civil Government, Morley's Universal Library, 2nd edition, George Routledge and Sons, London

stops.text: Adam Smith says a nation's wealth is what its people produce, not the gold in its treasury. Dividing work into special tasks makes each worker far more productive, and trade lets each person benefit from others' skills. People serving their own interest in a free market, he argues, are often led to serve the common good, though he also warned against businesses joining to fix prices.

quote.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
quote.author: Adam Smith
quote.ed: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (Project Gutenberg text)

stops.text: Marx and Engels argue that history is driven by struggles between classes. They praise modern industry for producing more than any earlier age, but claim it divides society into owners and workers who have nothing to sell but their labor. They call for workers to unite and overthrow this order, a call that later movements and their critics have argued over ever since.

quote.text: The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.
quote.author: Marx and Engels
quote.work: Manifesto of the Communist Party, Section I
quote.ed: authorized English translation, edited and annotated by Frederick Engels

stops.text: In Capital, Marx studies how money is turned into more money. He contrasts selling in order to buy with buying in order to sell at a profit. He argues that profit comes from workers' unpaid labor, a claim many economists accept in part and many reject.

quote.text: M—C—M, the transformation of money into commodities, and the change of commodities back again into money; or buying in order to sell.
quote.author: Marx
quote.ed: first American edition, Charles H. Kerr, Chicago

stops.text: Veblen notices that rich people often spend to show off, not because they need things. He calls it conspicuous consumption. Wealth wins respect, he says, only when others can see it.

quote.text: Conspicuous consumption of valuable goods is a means of reputability to the gentleman of leisure.
quote.author: Thorstein Veblen
quote.work: The Theory of the Leisure Class, Chapter IV (Conspicuous Consumption)
quote.ed: The Macmillan Company, New York (copyright 1899; 1908 printing)

stops.text: Tawney criticizes a society that treats getting rich as the main goal of life. He argues that property and industry should be judged by the service they do for others. Owning things is fine, he says, but owning without working is what corrupts.

quote.text: For it is not private ownership, but private ownership divorced from work, which is corrupting to the principle of industry.
quote.author: R. H. Tawney
quote.work: The Acquisitive Society, Chapter VI (The Functional Society)
quote.ed: Harcourt, Brace and Howe, New York

stops.text: Writing during the Great Depression, Keynes argues that a market economy can get stuck with many people out of work if total spending falls. He thought governments could help by spending and by managing interest rates. Economists still debate how far his ideas hold.

young: Wealth is having the things people need and want: food, homes, tools and money to trade for them. Money itself is just a handy way to trade, so you don't have to swap a chicken for a pair of shoes.

Adam Smith noticed that a baker bakes bread to earn a living, and that helps everyone get bread. Other writers worried that some people end up with far too much while others have too little. People still argue about the best way for wealth to be made and shared.
talk: Why is money useful? What would life be like without it?
Smith says the baker works for his own good and helps us too. Can you think of other examples?
Aristotle says there is such a thing as wanting too much money. What do you think?
Veblen says people buy things to show off. Have you seen that? Why do people do it?
If you earned ten dollars, how would you choose to spend, save or share it?
